note:
Refers to the entire book of Isaiah. “Vision” means that the book is a revelation from God.

**Isaiah.** “The Lord saves.”

**kings of Judah.** See Introduction: Date and Occasion. Isaiah’s prophetic career spanned at least the period from 740 B.C. (the year King Uzziah died) until 681 B.C., the death of Sennacherib.

Chapters 1, 3, and 5 depict a covenant lawsuit scene. Here an abbreviated historical prologue recalls the Lord’s good purposes, and an indictment follows. The whole of creation will bear witness against Israel that the Lord had warned them they would be judged if they broke their covenant with Him (Deut. 30:19; 32:1).

**.** The Hb. name “Yahweh” is usually represented in English translations as “Lord,” using small capitals. This name signifies the personal revelation of God to Israel and His solemn promise to be their God (Ex. 3:15).

**Children.** They were the Lord’s children by creation, by election, and by covenant (45:11; 49:7; 64:8; Deut. 32:6, 18; Mal. 2:10). The background for this is Moses’s writing in Deut. 32:1–9.

**rebelled.** Rebellion is willful transgression against the Lord’s sovereign and gracious rule (1:28; 43:27; 48:8; 59:13). Rebellious children could be subject to the death penalty (see Deut. 21:18–21).
Even unintelligent domestic animals know where their food comes from. Not so Judah.

An emphatic particle used in contexts of lament (1:4), but more often in threats (“woe”; cf. 3:9, 11; 5:11, 18, 20, 21). The staccato lament decries the folly and evil of God’s children.

**sinful nation.** At the exodus, Israel had been called to be a holy nation (Ex. 19:6). Rather than being “my people,” they are a people laden with iniquity. Rather than being God’s children, they are children who deal corruptly.

**the Holy One of Israel.** Isaiah’s special designation for the Lord calls attention to His unique and awe-inspiring splendor. The phrase occurs twenty-six times in Isaiah (e.g., 5:19, 24; 41:14, 16, 20; 60:9, 14). See also “the Holy One of Jacob” (29:23), “Holy One” (10:17; 40:25), and “your Holy One” (43:15).

Further preaching only hardens impenitent sinners. Sin is at its root irrational.

**1:5, 6 struck ... wounds.** The people were unable to recover from God’s chastisement. The imagery of the suffering nation has its counterpart in the suffering of God’s Servant (53:4, 5), who endured the judgment of God in His own body vicariously (that is, as a substitute for others). There are explicit verbal connections between the two passages., 6

A personification of Jerusalem. Zion was the hill that David captured (2 Sam. 5:7), but this Hb. idiom often stands for all of Jerusalem or even all of Judah and Israel.

**booth.** A temporary shelter used by watchmen during harvest to prevent valuable crops from being stolen or damaged by marauding animals. See note on 4:6.

A designation for God that presents Him as a divine warrior (13:4; 30:27; 40:10; 42:13, 25; 59:17; 66:15, 16), the commander over all troops whether in heaven or on earth. Ultimately, Israel’s survival is not due to the enemy’s weakness, but to God’s sovereign power.

**a few survivors.** The Lord will not overturn His promise. Even in the midst of judgment He will preserve a remnant. Paul quotes this verse in Rom. 9:29, presenting the idea of a remnant taken out of a larger group as an expression of the electing grace of God. In Rom. 9:27, Paul quotes from Isaiah’s teaching about the remnant at 10:20–23. See also Is. 4:3; 7:3 and note; 11:11, 12, 16; 28:5; 37:31, 32; 46:3.

**Sodom ... Gomorrah.** God’s people have become like the wicked inhabitants of Canaan, whose cities were destroyed (1:10; Gen. 18:20, 21; 19:24, 25). The fate of Sodom and Gomorrah typifies the terrible judgment of God on the kingdoms of this world (3:9; 13:19; Luke 17:28, 29; 2 Pet. 2:6–10; Jude 7; Rev. 11:8). Apart from Lot and his daughters, no one survived this judgment.

The central visible observances of OT religion. Although God ordered them to be performed, they were of no value without obedience from the heart (vv. 16, 17; 1 Sam. 15:22, 23; Ps. 51:16, 17; Mic. 6:6–8; Matt. 23:23).

**do not delight.** The Lord’s distaste for sacrifices offered by those who do evil (v. 16) is expressed with increasing sharpness: “I cannot endure” (v. 13); “my soul hates” (v. 14).
Although these festivals were required by God’s law, when performed merely as a ritual, they became an abomination to the Lord.

verse_quote: When you spread out your hands ... your hands are full of blood.
note: When the people of the ancient Near East prayed, they often spread out their hands as a gesture of petition. Yet in Judah’s case these same hands were stained with innocent blood: the people praying were implicated in the wider sins of their society. Their behavior hindered their prayers (cf. 1 P et. 3:7). They needed to wash themselves before they could come to a Holy God in prayer.
Concern for the needy is a practical demonstration of true godliness (v. 23; 58:7; Ps. 9:18 note; Jer. 22:16; James 1:27).

When a declaration of judgment is expected, the Lord issues a gracious offer of mediation. The language has legal overtones of attempting to resolve a dispute.

**scarlet.** Depicts hands “full of blood” (v. 15).

**white as snow.** God can take away the stain of sin without compromising His righteousness because Jesus Christ bore God’s punishment for sinners (53:4–6; Rom. 3:21–26).
God’s Word is a two-edged sword: eternal life (v. 19) or eternal death (v. 20; 66:24)., 20

Godliness is demonstrated by perseverance, stability, and consistency in doing God’s will. Through the purifying process, the Lord will renew a remnant who will again constitute a “faithful city” (v. 26), for He is faithful (49:7; 55:3).

**whore.** The metaphor shifts from unfaithful children to an unfaithful wife. A whore in religion is an idolater, someone who has forsaken God to serve idols (Jer. 2:20; 3:1; Ezek. 16:23–30; Hos. 2:2; 3:1). The sins listed (vv. 21–23) are evidence that God’s people have forsaken Him.

**justice ... Righteousness.** Justice means right relations between people. It is violated by murder, rebellion, stealing, and bribery (vv. 21–23). True justice will defend the cause of orphans and widows as much as the cause of those who can pay bribes and give rewards. The enemies of justice may even pass laws that facilitate their wrongdoing (10:1). These are specific examples of the “scarlet sins” mentioned in v.18. Despite all such obstacles, God promises to restore righteousness to the earth (v. 26; 32:1; 33:5, 6; 42:1–4).
Represent Jerusalem’s unjust rulers (v. 23). Silver contaminated with dross and watered-down wine are symbols of spiritual pollution and impurity.
God’s law strongly condemns bribery, which fosters injustice and discrimination (5:23; cf. Ex. 23:8; Deut. 16:19).

verse_quote: the LORD of hosts, the Mighty One of Israel.
note: The lengthy and exalted title focuses on the Lord’s power. God, the Sovereign, will restore justice by removing His enemies, the unrighteous leaders of Jerusalem. It is striking that the Lord’s enemies are among His own people.

The new age will be a restoration, bringing miraculous continuation and renewal to the covenant community. A purified leadership and people will live in harmony with God’s will (24:23; 32:1).

**city of righteousness.** The new community is made up of men and women who practice righteousness and demonstrate a commitment to God and to other human beings (1:21 note).

The righteous and faithful city is identified as Zion rather than Jerusalem, a title that emphasizes the spiritual purpose of Jerusalem as the home of the temple.

**redeemed.** Ransomed, transferred, or freed from ownership by another through the payment of a price. The penitent, who turn their backs on idolatry and injustice, find freedom from Satan, sin, and death through the righteousness of Christ imputed to them.

What people hold in honor will be exposed as worthless. Sinners will see how wrong they have been when they come to ruin (26:11; 44:9, 11; 65:13; 66:5).

**oaks ... gardens.** Places of fertility rites and pagan worship that the people have chosen in preference to serving God (65:3 and note; 66:17).

Drought and fire are metaphors for judgment. Water in Isaiah signifies free, gracious, and bountiful salvation (11:9; 32:2; 41:18; 55:1; 58:11). The absence of water signifies separation from God’s blessings (3:1; 50:2). It is a particularly apt image because what the fertility rites promised to deliver was the much-needed rain. They were incapable of doing so, as the Lord made clear in the days of Elijah (see 1 Kin. 17; 18).

See note on 4:4. Unlike the purifying judgment of fire in v. 25, for some the Lord’s judgment will simply be destructive. There is redemption for those who repent but ruin for those who persist in their rebellion.

–**4** An oracle almost identical to Mic. 4:1–3. Isaiah and Micah were contemporaries, so it is not surprising that their messages would have significant overlap. Since the Lord was the ultimate author, He could deliver His revelation to His messengers directly or through another legitimate prophet.

**2:2 in the latter days.** An indefinite reference that may include a lengthy process of fulfillment, including the reigns of Hezekiah and Josiah, the period of restoration after the exile, the first coming of our Lord, the present age, and the glorious consummation (Jer. 23:20; 30:24; Ezek. 38:8, 16; Hos. 3:5). The phrase designates a new epoch that for the prophet lies in the hidden future. The new epoch alters history in every dimension and is the goal toward which events are striving. The apostle Peter relates this time to the new age begun at Pentecost by using the phrase for an introduction to his citation of Joel 2:28–32 (Acts 2:17).

**mountain.** The Temple Mount is a metaphor for the Lord’s kingdom that will be exalted above all other kingdoms (cf. 11:9; 65:25; 66:20). Mount Zion and the temple on it were symbols of heaven and the heavenly sanctuary (Heb. 9:24). These earthly representations have passed away (Heb. 8:13); through the priesthood of the ascended Lord, the church comes directly to the heavenly reality (Heb. 12:22–24).

**highest of the mountains.** Pagans worshiped their gods at mountain shrines. Israel’s God, who is worshiped on Mount Zion, will establish Himself in the eyes of all races and nations as the only true and living God, even as He is worshiped today. Although Mount Zion was not physically imposing, its spiritual significance was out of all proportion to its size. See note on Ps. 48:2.

They encourage one another to worship God from regenerate hearts (John 3:3–8).

**out of Zion.** The prophet proclaims the new era in which Jews and Gentiles will serve one King (11:10–12; 27:13; 56:3–8; 66:19–23). Zion, or Jerusalem, stands for God’s throne (1:8 note).

**the law ... the word of the** LORD**.** Represent the media of revelation that belong to the priest and the prophet respectively. The scenario depicts a radical transformation from the situation in 1:3, where Israel herself does not know the Lord’s word.

In this renewed Jerusalem, the Lord will establish the justice that has been so lacking, not only for His own people but for the whole world (see 1:27). The redemption of Israel takes place through the salvation of the nations, not their destruction (cf. Ps. 47).

**swords into plowshares.** Cf. Joel 3:10. The instruments of war are transformed into implements of human flourishing.

Stands for God’s blessings, presence, and revelation (9:2; 30:26; 42:6, 16; 60:1–3). The Lord is the light in blessing and in judgment (10:17; 60:19, 20; cf. John 1:4; 8:12). People who exchange His light for the darkness of their corrupt minds (5:20; 8:20), will experience His judgment and live in the darkness of separation from God (5:30; 13:10; 59:9; cf. John 3:19, 20). Isaiah’s message to his original audience is that if the peoples of the world will walk in the Lord’s ways in the last days (v. 3), should not the house of Judah walk in the light now?

Isaiah condemns syncretism, the mixture of religions. These verses contrast the light with all the things the people have adopted from the nations: magic, greed, warfare, and idolatry. The key words are “full” or “filled.”

**2:6 things from the east ... Philistines.** The pagan cultures on either side of Judah. Philistia was to the west; Babylon and Assyria were to the east. The law condemns all forms of magic and divination (Lev. 19:26; Deut. 18:10, 11). Such abominations finally lead the Lord to abandon His people.

They relied on their own military strength (30:16; 31:1, 3), as well as alliances with foreign nations (see v. 6), rather than on the Lord (Ps. 20:7). Israel’s kings were forbidden to multiply horses and chariots (Deut. 17:14–20), though Solomon was probably the worst offender in this respect (see 1 Kin. 10:26).
Isaiah contrasts the powerlessness of human-created idols with the power of the uncreated God in 44:6–20.

At God’s judgment people may seek shelter, but no one can hide from Him (Rev. 6:16).

**the terror of the** LORD**.** The Lord is far more awe-inspiring and fear-provoking than the Assyrian kings, despite the claims they made in their annals that their appearance induced terror in their enemies.

The contrast between the exalted God and the weakness of humanity is a central theme in Isaiah’s call narrative (Is. 6).

**in that day.** The day of the Lord brings judgment on the godless, but blessing and salvation to the godly (Joel 2:31; Zeph. 1:7; 2:13–18). Isaiah’s reference encompasses historical events (the fall of Israel, Assyria, Judah) and the coming judgment and salvation (3:7; 7:18–25; 11:10, 11; 24:21; 27:1).

verse_quote: cedars of Lebanon ... oaks of Bashan.
note: Large, impressive trees with valuable wood (Ezek. 27:5, 6). They symbolize the permanence and splendor of nature and are natural symbols for pride (cf. Ezek. 31; Dan. 4). But just as the mighty cedar can be felled, the most exalted human beings are subject to God’s judgment.
Symbolize pride at being first in trade and commerce (23:1, 8).
See note on 2:11.

verse_quote: to the moles and to the bats.
note: As terrified humans seek refuge from divine wrath by hiding in holes in the ground and caves, they will discard their idols to the subterranean creatures that surround them.

One must trust God, who gives breath, not those who are dependent on Him. In the face of many very real dangers on all sides, the Judean kings were often tempted to trust in human allies rather than in the Lord (see Is. 7).
The chaotic conditions result in a lack of the most basic supplies of food and water. See note on 1:30.
The Lord will remove every kind of leader that Isaiah’s audience is trusting to secure their society: warriors, sages, magicians, and other prominent people. See note on 11:2., 3
Because they have trusted in their leaders rather than in God, the nation will be ruled by inexperienced people who are unable to govern wisely. A fitting punishment.
The collapse of civilization comes with communal strife: rich against poor; young against old. Normal social structures will be overthrown.

In a collapsing society, someone who has as little as a decent suit of clothes will seem prosperous enough to be made a ruler. But when the people try to draft such a person, he will reply that his wealth is only an illusion; he has no better answers than they have.
The fall of Jerusalem (586 B.C.) was a partial fulfillment of this prophecy, as was the devastation caused by Sennacherib’s siege of the city in 701 B.C.
Israel has no sense of shame, defying God and acting as if the covenant does not exist. See 1:9, 10.
Even though both righteous and wicked alike are affected by the siege and fall of Jerusalem, the Lord distinguishes between these two groups., 11

As in v. 4, the punishment for trusting in human leaders is the replacement of those leaders by unprepared and ill-equipped stand-ins.

**O my people.** See note on 40:1. On the lack of leadership and its consequences, see 3:4–7 and notes.

In the OT, the metaphor of a vineyard is an important symbol for the temple, temple city, or even the entire Land of Promise. Israel can therefore be referred to as God’s vine or vineyard (e.g., Ps. 80; Is. 5:1–7; 27: 2–6; Jer. 12:10; Ezek. 15; 17:3–10; 19:10–12; Hos. 9:10; 10:1). The Lord’s people are His vineyard, yet those He has placed in leadership over the vineyard have neglected and abused it.
Cf. the actions of these rulers with those of the ideal Davidic king in 11:3–5.

These women live to the fullest, flaunting their wealth at the expense of those around them. The ornaments are meant to impress others and to supply magical protection from sudden disaster. This outward adornment reflects an inner attitude of pride and self-sufficiency (1 Pet. 3:3, 4). It is the feminine equivalent of the confidence that the men place in their extensive supply of leaders (3:2, 3). Both groups will be stripped of the things in which they place their trust.

The destitution threatened by the day of the Lord is expressed with words associated with bloodshed, war, and captivity. Far from having an abundance of unnecessary ornaments, in that day the women will lack the basic necessities of bread, clothing, and a husband.
Jerusalem is personified and joins in the lament.
The day of judgment. See note on 2:11.

The term has two possible senses. One is literal, corresponding to the parallel phrase “fruit of the land.” In this case it is speaking of a glorious restoration of the remnant of God’s people on the day when the Lord acts. However, Hebrew parallelism is not always synonymous but often has an “and what’s more” character. The other possible sense of “branch” is as a messianic title: Jesus Christ is the fulfillment of the promise as He yields glorious spiritual fruit (11:1–5; Jer. 23:5; Zech. 3:8; John 15:1–8). The remnant find life and blessing in Him (6:13). Because Jesus humbled Himself, He is crowned with glory (52:13; 53:12; Phil. 2:9–11). This verse and the ones that immediately follow provide an important background for chs. 5 and 7, where the vineyard of the Lord is treated in greater depth. Note that 4:2–6 conveys the idea that the Lord’s faithful remnant will be called holy.

**glorious.** Displaying the splendor and brightness of God. The glory of God is revealed in all His works, but especially in the Messiah (Ps. 19:1; John 1:18).

**the survivors.** A remnant (1:9 note).

Represents Jerusalem as a whole. See note on 1:8.

**holy.** Consecrated to God, the Holy One of Israel (1:4 note; 62:12). Holiness is a key theme in Isaiah (see ch. 6).

**recorded.** Their names are written in the book of life (Ex. 32:32, 33; Ps. 69:28; Dan. 12:1; Rev. 20:12).

verse_quote: when the Lord shall have washed away the filth ... and cleansed.
note:
This judgment will be one of purging, a theme that will appear again in ch. 27.

**daughters of Zion.** Wealthy women who flaunted their affluence. See note on 3:16.

**spirit.** Possibly this is the Holy Spirit, but more likely it refers to the process of purification (cf. 28:6).

**burning.** Signifies judgment (1:25–31; 10:17; 30:27; 42:25). Through the process of refining fire, consuming the faithless and purifying the faithful, God will produce a holy Zion.

In the new act of redemption, the Creator of heaven and earth (40:26; 42:5; 45:12, 18) will renew everything for the sake of His people. God gives the glory of the messianic age; it does not come from human effort or skill (Jon. 2:9; Eph. 2:4–10). A significant theme in this chapter is God’s act of recreating His people and being their dwelling place.

**cloud ... smoke ... shining of a flaming fire.** Unlike the burning of the fire of judgment in v. 4, this cloud and fire signal God’s protective presence, as at the Red Sea (Ex. 13:20–22), over the tabernacle (Ex. 40:34–38), and in the wilderness (Num. 9:15–23). Here His presence covers a restored and sanctified Mount Zion (2:2 note).

**a canopy.** Jewish weddings include a canopy over the bride and bridegroom as part of the ceremony (see Joel 2:16).

The annual Feast of Booths recalled Israel’s wandering in the wilderness and the temporary shelters that they lived in during that time. The Lord will once again provide for His people’s needs as He did in the past.

**shade.** God protects His people. See note on 30:2.

**refuge.** In contrast to human deceptions (28:15, 17), the Lord provides effective shelter from the storm (25:4; cf. Pss. 14:6; 46:1; 62:7; 94:22).

Cf. 3:14 note. This vineyard song should be read with the one in ch. 27.The owner and the vineyard stand for God and His people, though that would not have been obvious at first hearing. The language is reminiscent of Song of Songs (e.g., Song 2:15, 16). The song is ultimately fulfilled in Jesus Christ, who replaces sour grapes with new fruit (Matt. 21:33–44; John 15:1–6).

Images that reinforce the expectation of an abundant harvest; the vineyard is protected against pests and intruders (see Song 2:15). Any deficiency in the harvest is therefore due to the grape vines themselves.

**wild grapes.** Lit. “stinking or sour things.”

God decrees desolation and destruction for His people by removing their hedge of protection because of their unfaithfulness and unfruitfulness. God will withdraw His covenant protection from them (cf. Matt. 21:40, 41).

The weeds represent God’s curse (7:23–25; 32:13), that is, the anarchy following war (3:4, 5). God can also turn curse into blessing, replacing the briers and thorns with the pine tree and myrtle (55:13).

**no rain.** Rain in its proper season is a covenant blessing, while drought is a covenant curse (see Deut. 11:17).

See note on 1:9.

**justice ... bloodshed ... righteousness ... an outcry.** The last words in each line rhyme in Hebrew.

The first of six exclamations of woe, proclaiming God’s displeasure with greed, drunkenness, and other sins. The first woe condemns greed.

**add field to field.** The land belonged to God (Lev. 25:23), had been allotted to specific families by patrimony (Num. 33:54), and was the basis of livelihood. Deprived of their land, small farmers in Israel were forced to become day laborers or slaves.
God’s judgment targets the rich in their greed and self-indulgence. They were not content with a modest living. Mansions provide no protection from His eye (24:10 note).

The bath is a liquid measure of about six gallons. In comparison to its size, the vineyard will produce practically nothing. Likewise, a homer of seed (six bushels) yields only an ephah (half a bushel) of produce. The land will be cursed. Instead of their vast landholding yielding increased profits, the land would produce little (Deut. 28:38, 39).

The second woe condemns drunkenness. See note on 24:11. Although wine was a common beverage in times when water was not safe to drink, overindulgence is a characteristic of social corruption and moral laxity (chs. 22, 28; Amos 4:1–3; 6:6, 7). It is clear that other people are doing the work on the large estates while the landowners sit back and expected to reap the profits.

See note on 40:1.

**exile.** The exile with all its miseries is threatened as a judgment on the people, who have shown no knowledge of the right way to behave.

Lit. “the grave,” used almost exclusively in poetry. See Prov. 9:18 and note. Isaiah portrays death as a terrible beast that devours everyone without regard to social class, both the “honored” and the “multitude” (v. 13). In Isaiah, “Sheol” often emphasizes the notion of a shadowy place of nonlife that constantly threatens the unfaithful.
See note on 1:21. The contrast between God and His people is immense even though they are supposed to be a holy people (Ex. 19:6).

The third woe condemns those who mock God as they sin. It imagines them dragging a load of their own sin that is so heavy that they need a cart just to contain it, even while they scoff at the idea that the Lord will act to judge sin. They misconstrue God’s patience (2 Pet. 3:3, 4).
A favorite title for God in Isaiah. See note on 1:4.

The fourth woe condemns moral corruption that reverses good and evil.

**darkness ... light.** See notes on 2:5 and 5:30.

The fifth woe condemns pride and self-righteousness.

**wise in their own eyes.** An expression for irrational, arrogant autonomy. A revelation from God, who alone knows all things, is the only firm foundation for knowledge (Prov. 1:7).

The sixth woe condemns those who pervert justice.

**mixing strong drink.** Refers to wine and beer with spices added. Once again, as in 5:11, Isaiah speaks of overindulgence. These men are skilled in preparing exotic drinks, but they neglect weighty matters like guilt and innocence.
See note on 1:23. Bribery involves injustice and greed, as in 5:8.

See note on “burning” at 4:4. In a dry climate, the merest spark is enough to set the stubble ablaze at certain times of the year.

**the law ... the word.** These are central in Isaiah’s vision of the latter days (see 2:3), but God’s own people reject them.

At the revelation of God’s anger, nature quakes (2:19; 13:13; 24:18, 19; Ezek. 32:6–8 note). For a contrasting image of redemption, see 54:10.

**streets.** See note on 24:11.

**his anger has not turned away.** God is not reconciled, and His wrath hangs over the disobedient (9:12, 17, 21; 10:4; 31:3).

This description of the Assyrian army closely matches its portrayal on ancient Assyrian reliefs.

**5:26 signal.** A signal flag (11:10, 12; 18:3; 49:22; 62:10). Like a commander in battle, the Lord summons the nations to execute His judgment (10:5). Like a pet dog, they come at His whistle.

**nations far away.** Egypt, Assyria, and Babylon. The imperial Assyrian army was made up of mercenaries hired from all over the Assyrian Empire. The professionalism of such mercenary armies would have been terrifying to militia armies such as Judah’s.

See note on 2:11.

**darkness.** The people who once possessed the light (2:5) are now walking in great darkness. This metaphor for depression, alienation, and judgment (8:22; 42:7; 47:5; 60:2) teaches that all who twist justice by living in darkness (5:20; 29:15) will suffer the darkness of God’s judgment. By contrast, the light of God will dawn on the needy (9:2; 29:18; 42:7; 49:9; 58:10; 60:1, 2). The Lord is sovereign over darkness and light (45:7).

**distress.** Lit. “sorrow,” “narrowness.” God delivers His own from such confinement (25:4; 63:9).

Having suffered from leprosy (2 Chr. 26:16–21), he died in 740 B.C., signaling the end of a long period of relative peace and prosperity.

**I saw.** Isaiah describes a “theophany,” a visible manifestation of God. God’s coming is often attended by such phenomena as earthquakes, smoke, fire, and lightning (13:3 note; 29:6; 30:27–31; Ex. 19:18, 19; Pss. 18:7–15; 50:3; 97:2; Mic. 1:3, 4; Nah. 1:3–8; Hab. 3:3–15).

**the Lord.** _Adonai,_ lit. “Sovereign.” Cf. note on 1:2.

**throne.** The Lord rules heaven and earth from His throne. The death of the earthly king did not affect the ultimate fate of the universe. The choir of seraphim (6:2 note) and the splendor of God’s holiness inspired the prophet throughout his ministry.

**the train of his robe.** The very edge of His garment was greater than the temple.

**the temple.** The heavenly temple, after which the temple in Jerusalem was patterned (cf. Rev. 4:1–8).

A Hb. word probably meaning “burning ones” (cf. the fiery serpents in Num. 21:6). Representations of angelic creatures with six wings have been discovered in the Near East by archaeologists.

**covered his face.** The seraphim have no glory to compare with God’s, and they cannot look on Him directly.

**covered his feet.** “Feet” can also be translated “legs.” This may be an indication of modesty.

**flew.** The seraph does the Sovereign’s will. Here it is to praise Him.

A threefold repetition is the strongest sort of superlative. It is the only one of God’s attributes that is repeated in this way. Nothing is as holy as God. See note on 1:4.

**of hosts.** Originally a military title, its scope is extended to denote divine control over all the created realm. See note on 1:9.

**whole earth.** This announcement explains the cosmic perspective of the prophet. God is King of the world, and His salvation and judgment extend to all nations (11:4, 9, 12; 42:1, 4, 5; 65:17; 66:1; cf. Luke 2:14).

**glory.** See note on 4:2, “glorious.” God’s glory filled the earthly tabernacle and temple at key moments of the dedication ceremonies, representing the Lord symbolically taking up residence there (Ex. 40:35; 1 Kin. 8:11). The whole earth is full of God’s glory because He indwells the whole cosmos, not merely a small building on Mount Zion.

Isaiah is astonished by the glory of God; like Peter he becomes afraid (cf. Luke 5:8). He pronounces an oracular curse upon himself. His conviction of sin is specific: he has unclean lips. The fact that others around him suffer from the same condition compounds his sin rather than alleviating it.

The altar from which the live coal is taken is not described. The stress is on the purification necessary for approaching God. The altar symbolizes purification by blood, and the fire, purification by the Spirit. The blood of Christ and the ministry of the Holy Spirit sanctify believers today.
The purification is specifically applied to the point of his sin—his lips—making the prophet acceptable as a minister of God’s words (Jer. 1:9).

The Lord permits Isaiah to listen in on the sessions of the royal, heavenly court (“us”). From this moment on, Isaiah is a servant of God’s court and proclaims God’s message to kings and people alike (cf. 1 Kin. 22:19, 20; Jer. 23:18, 22). Having been freely forgiven, Isaiah volunteers without waiting to hear the nature of his commission.

Isaiah’s mission is paradoxical in its effect, as is the proclamation of the Word of God (Matt. 13:13–15; Rom. 11:7–10, 25). The prophetic word closes the way of God to those who are rebellious, proud, and hypocritical (29:13–16; 65:1–7), but opens it to the deaf, blind, humble, and poor (29:18, 19).
Isaiah is asking how long the message of judgment must go forth until he can be a “herald of good news” (40:9).

The land will be laid waste, and even the remnant who will be saved will be further purified by suffering (1:9 note).

**stump.** The Middle Eastern terebinth and oak trees can produce new shoots even when they appear to have been cut or damaged beyond all hope. There is a glimmer of hope for God’s people, but it is only to be found on the far side of judgment.

Oracles of judgment and hope associated with the war between Judah and a coalition of Israel and Syria (734–732 B.C.). Ahaz, king of Judah, was seriously threatened by the alliance of Pekah, king of Israel, with Rezin, king of Syria (2 Kin. 16:5–18; 2 Chr. 28:16–21). They threatened to invade Judah if Ahaz would not help them against Assyria.

This expression means the current head of the house, Ahaz. It recalls the Lord’s covenant with David, granting him an eternal offspring and kingdom (2 Sam. 7:12–16). The attempt to replace his dynasty with another (“the son of Tabeel,” v. 6) cannot succeed because God’s promises are at stake. The rival claimant doesn’t even deserve to be mentioned by name in the text.

**shook.** Ahaz, the proud king, has been unable to calm his people. The response of the leader has created panic among the people (22:3 note).

“A remnant shall return” (10:20–22) is a name representing a promise of salvation and life for the faithful beyond the imminent doom of the unfaithful. Judah may suffer, but a remnant will remain (see 6:13).

**the conduit of the upper pool.** Water supplies are crucial in case of a siege of the city.
Two kingdoms are about to be destroyed: Damascus in 732 B.C. by Tiglath-pileser III, and Samaria in 722 B.C. by Sargon II.

GOD**.** This title combines the Hb. word for “lord, sovereign” with the covenant name Yahweh, represented by “God,” using small capitals (cf. 25:8; 28:16; 40:10; 52:4; 65:13).

**shall not come to pass.** The Lord voids the counsel of kings (8:9, 10; 40:23; Ps. 33:10, 11).

That is, less than the span of a normal human life (see Ps. 90:10). God will fulfill His promises after Ahaz’s death (2 Kin. 17:24–41). The northern kingdom will actually be conquered by the Assyrians much sooner than that.

A play on different meanings of the same Hb. word. Faith means knowing God’s promise, assenting to it intellectually, and trusting Him to keep it. The threat to Ahaz’s kingdom provides him an opportunity for him to trust in God and see God deliver him.

A sign will authenticate the prophetic message concerning the future. Normally, asking for a sign is a mark of weak faith (as in the case of Gideon in Judg. 6); however, here God condescends to Ahaz’s weakness and offers him a sign.

**deep ... high.** Nothing is outside the Lord’s sovereignty; no sign is too great for Him to accomplish (Deut. 10:14; Ps. 139:8; Rom. 8:39).

**I will not put the LORD to the test.** Ahaz makes his refusal sound spiritual, quoting Deut. 6:16, but in reality he has already made up his mind to place his faith in the chariots and horsemen of Assyria rather than in the Lord.
See note on 7:2.

This Hb. word occurs seven times in the OT. It means a young woman of marriageable age, who in ancient Judah and Israel was normally a virgin (Gen. 24:43). The Septuagint translates the Hb. word with a Gk. term that specifically means “virgin.” The NT understands the ultimate fulfillment of Isaiah’s promise to be the Virgin Mary (Matt. 1:23).

**Immanuel.** “God with us.” Conveys God’s promise to save, bless, and protect His children. The identities of the virgin and the child have been the subject of considerable discussion, and three major interpretations exist. First, some find the prophecy exclusively fulfilled in the prophet’s own lifetime. Some of these interpreters, especially Jews of the second century A.D., have understood the prophecy to mean Ahaz’s wife and her child, Hezekiah (2 Kin. 18:2). But, as Jerome (c. A.D. 400) pointed out, Hezekiah was already born. Others identify the woman as Isaiah’s wife or a woman betrothed to him (8:3). The child is then Isaiah’s son, Maher-shalal-hash-baz. However, the Hb. term translated “virgin” would not normally be used for a woman who was already a mother (of Shear-jashub, 7:3). If it means someone engaged to the prophet, then one must assume that his first wife had died prior to this prophecy. Further, this interpretation requires that the child have two different names: “God Is with Us” (Immanuel) and “The Spoil Speeds, the Prey Hastens” (Maher-shalal-hash-baz; cf. 8:3). In that case, the point of the immediate fulfillment would be that God’s presence with His people brings judgment as well as salvation. Second, in the light of the NT, the traditional Christian interpretation identifies the child directly as the Messiah, a divine personage whose birth is above nature (and so of the same miraculous order as the sign of v. 11). This approach equates the child named “Immanuel” with the child possessing God’s titles in 9:6, and with the “branch” of ch. 11. According to Matthew, the virgin is Mary and the child is Jesus Christ (Matt. 1:22, 23). However, v. 16 seems to require the birth to be imminent. A third interpretation is to consider the prophecy to be typological, with a two-stage fulfillment: an immediate but partial realization in Isaiah’s day and a later definitive one in the birth of Jesus Christ, who secures God’s throne forever. The difficulty that remains is determining the partial fulfillment. Some opt for the birth of Isaiah’s son Maher-shalal-hash-baz (8:1–3), while others take the initial reference to be to a nameless teenage mother, who hears and believes God’s promises and thus names her son “God Is with Us” in spite of the threatening circumstances. Her faith contrasts with the conduct of King Ahaz, the son of David who refuses to trust God’s promise entirely, but an ordinary birth falls short of the radical nature of the sign envisaged in v. 11.

Not typical food for infants, but they point to a time when people will have to live off unworked fields (v. 22). The child is identified with the remnant.

**when he knows how to refuse the evil.** The boy is not just able to distinguish between right and wrong, but he actively chooses what is right, in contrast to the failed leadership of Israel that has been insensitive to social and spiritual values (5:11–23). What is true of this child in an imperfect and lesser way is perfectly and fully true of Jesus Christ (42:1–4).

Before the time required for a child to reach an age of adult moral accountability—twelve years—Pekah and Remaliah will both be defeated. In this understanding, “boy” points primarily to Isaiah’s son and secondarily to Christ.
The consequences of Ahaz’s unbelieving trust in Assyria will be devastating not only for Syria and Israel, but for Judah as well.

See note on 2:11. The fall of Damascus, of Samaria, and the devastation of Judah are foretastes of the events of the last judgment.

**fly ... bee.** These insects swarm in great numbers, like the hordes of invaders.
Traditional hiding places will provide no escape (2:19).

Shaving the head is a sign of mourning (15:2) and a way of humiliating conquered enemies (2 Sam. 10:4, 5). It is a way of systematically “de-manning” the captives, which is why the “feet” (the lower part of the anatomy from the waist down) is also shaved. Ahaz has hired Tiglath-pileser of Assyria to help him against Syria and Israel, but the Lord will use Assyria to humiliate Judah instead (v. 17).

The land will be so depopulated that this limited food will seem abundant.

**curds and honey.** See note on v. 15. The remnant will have something to eat, but it will not be much.
The cultivated land will return to weeds and be barely fit for grazing. This represents God’s covenant curse on the land (see 5:6 note).
Probably a polished piece of wood like a signboard. The meaning of the name is explained in v. 4.
Two witnesses are necessary to attest to legal documents or transactions.

Isaiah refers to his wife in this way perhaps because of her association with him as a prophet, or perhaps because she was a prophet in her own right (Judg. 4:4; 2 Kin. 22:14).

**Maher-shalal-hash-baz.** The name means “the spoil speeds, the prey hastens,” which signifies the rapid devastation of Syria, Israel, and Judah, but also the presence of God with the remnant and the impending fulfillment of God’s word of promise. The similarities between the sign of his birth and the sign of Immanuel are striking, perhaps because his birth is an immediate testimony to God’s long-term promise.

Judah.

**waters of Shiloah.** Might refer to a stream flowing from the Gihon Spring (2 Chr. 32:30). It is a symbol of the Lord’s faithful but unspectacular provision, which the people have despised (cf. 1:30 note; Jer. 2:13; Zech. 4:10).

**rejoice.** The people may be looking forward to the fall of Rezin, king of Syria, without considering that the word of judgment applies to Judah as well.

The Euphrates, standing for the Assyrian invaders. The mighty Euphrates contrasts with the soft waters of Shiloah (v. 6). In Isaiah’s day, it regularly burst its banks and flooded the surrounding area of Mesopotamia.

The implication is that Assyria will almost, but not quite, annihilate Judah. At the height of the Assyrian invasion in 701 B.C., Jerusalem escapes, but barely (37:33–36).

**O Immanuel.** See v. 10; note on 7:14. Isaiah bestows the name of the virgin’s child on Judah as the object of God’s care.
Syria and Israel.

See note on 11:2.

**God is with us.** Hb. “Immanuel.” God is with the remnant of Judah, which will not be destroyed (v. 8 notes; 7:14 note).
Isaiah has had an experience of inner compulsion from the Spirit of God (Ezek. 1:3; 3:14).
The people considered Isaiah a traitor because he said that Ahaz and his administration were wrong to rely on Assyria.

It is not people (v. 12), but the Lord who is the object of fear. The kings of Syria and Israel seem dangerous to Judah but the Lord can bring their threat to nothing. Even Assyria can do nothing without the Lord’s permission. He is the ultimate authority to whom all must submit, in whom all must trust, and to whom everyone must render an account (12:2; 33:6; 50:10; 59:19; Pss. 25:12–15; 34:11–14).

A place of refuge.

**a stone of offense.** The sign of Immanuel, which Ahaz rejected, will be a vital test of faith. To those who trust the Lord and believe His promise, He will be a sanctuary. But those who refuse to trust in the Lord will stumble over this sign.

**both houses.** Judah and Israel.

This could refer to God’s revelation (1:10) to Moses (Deut. 4:44, 45), to Isaiah, or to both.

**disciples.** Isaiah’s followers are to write down and seal his prophecy like a law so that it can be known later whether it fails or is fulfilled by events (vv. 1, 2, 20). This is the test of a true prophet (Deut. 18:21, 22; Jer. 28:9), through whom God is known and trusted. In the midst of the destruction, God preserves the holy seed (see 6:13).

See 25:9; 26:8; 30:18; 33:2; 40:31; 49:23; 64:4.

**hiding his face.** The covenant God, who is presently leaving His people to themselves, is also free in bestowing grace on those who repent (54:8; 64:7; Deut. 31:18; 32:20).
The children’s names are significant (7:3; 8:1, 3 and notes).

God’s law prohibits diviners (Is. 2:6 note).

**chirp and mutter.** The mediums promise contact with the dead, who in the popular understanding of Judah are insubstantial and weak-voiced. Isaiah regards calling on them as contemptible, as well as useless.

See note on 8:16.

**dawn.** Light stands for God’s blessing. See note on 2:5.
An image of despair (5:30 note; 50:10).
Being in the north, these regions in Galilee were the first to suffer from the Assyrian invasion of 732 B.C. (2 Kin. 15:29).

See note on 2:5.

**deep darkness.** The Assyrians cast their terrible shadow over the land and the people (cf. Pss. 23:4; 44:19; 107:10). Yet there is hope; the certainty of that hope is expressed in the “prophetic perfect” (“have seen”), speaking of the future light as if it has already happened.
God opens up a new future for the humble (29:19) where gloom had previously existed (35:10; 51:3; 61:7). This new joy finds expression in the metaphors of harvest and of victory (cf. 5:10; 8:4).

Figures of oppression (10:27; 14:25; 47:6; cf. Matt. 11:29, 30).

**day of Midian.** A reference to Gideon’s defeat of the Midianites, which was accomplished by God’s mighty power in spite of Gideon’s own weakness (10:26, 27; Judg. 6:7; 7:22–25).
The debris left from battle can be removed and burned when the fighting stops. God will bring an end to war (2:4; Ps. 46:9, 10; 2 Cor. 10:4).

The good news is the birth of Jesus Christ. The four royal names express both His divine and human qualities, giving assurance that He is indeed “Immanuel” (7:14).

**born ... given.** The verbs are consistent with His humanity and deity respectively.

**the government shall be upon his shoulder.** He will carry the burden of rule and authority (cf. 22:22).

**Wonderful Counselor.** “Wonderful” might be more accurately translated “miraculous” because it typically describes God’s mighty works. The role of a counselor is to provide wisdom (Jer. 18:18). This coming King will possess divine wisdom.

**Mighty God.** As a warrior, God protects His people (10:21; Deut. 10:17; Jer. 32:18). This attribute of divine power is ascribed to the coming King. For the importance of this verse in the interpretation of the Seventy Weeks passage, see note on Dan. 9:27.

**Everlasting Father.** The coming King possesses divine eternity: He is from ancient times, and He will not need a successor to follow in His footsteps (cf. 2 Sam. 7:13; Mic. 5:2). Ancient kings often referred to themselves as the fathers of their subjects. This name reveals the divine, eternal care that the coming King will have for His people.

**Prince of Peace.** His government brings divine peace to the earth (2:4; 11:6–9; Ps. 72:7; Zech. 9:10; Luke 2:14).

He is a descendant of David (11:1 note), and he will establish the kingdom of God in “justice and with righteousness” (1:21 note); his reign will endure forever. No earthly son of David, such as Hezekiah or Josiah, ever lived up to this grand description.

**zeal.** God guarantees that He Himself will fulfill this promise; it will not depend on human power or decisions (37:32; 42:13; Zech. 1:14).
The Lord will judge Israel (the northern kingdom) and its capital, Samaria. The northern kingdom is also sometimes called Ephraim. (Judah is the southern kingdom, with Jerusalem as its capital.)
Their motivation has been to preserve and glorify themselves. Compare also their words “we will ... we will” in v. 10 (Gen. 11:3, 4; Is. 5:21).

The people think the challenges they face are minor setbacks rather than the beginning of the end. They imagine that they are going to start rebuilding with better materials, when in reality destruction lies ahead.

The Assyrians (7:1 note; 7:20 note; 8:7 note) would attack Syria from the north, and the Syrians and the Philistines would attack Israel from the east and west, respectively. The Lord will raise up many enemies.

**9:12 his anger has not turned away.** This refrain is also found in 9:17, 21; 10:4 (cf. 31:3). See note on 5:25. The hand that once delivered Israel from the Egyptians is now extended to strike His own people.

They have been unresponsive to divine discipline (Amos 4:6, 8–11). They have not depended on the Lord or sought Him with diligence; instead, they have persisted in their rebellion (8:19; 11:10; 31:1; 55:6; 58:2; 65:10).

Represent the civil and religious leadership, as explained in v. 15 (cf. 3:1–3; 30:10 note). The same imagery, including the “palm branch and reed,” is used to represent Egyptian leaders in 19:15. Because they are opposites, they also imply judgment for everyone else in between.

See note on 1:17. The gravity of God’s anger is vividly expressed when it is said that He will have no mercy on the fatherless and widows. Not even the most helpless members of society will escape.

**everyone is godless and an evildoer.** Sin is found in every person, even the fatherless and widow, and it corrupts both their thoughts and their deeds (Gen. 6:5; 8:21). The Lord’s total destruction is just.

Pride, narcissism, and greed destroy the fiber of society, especially the covenant relationship among the tribes. Before the revelation of this oracle, Manasseh fought Ephraim (Judg. 12:4), and together they battled Judah during the war with Israel and Syria. Sin is self-destructive: as a fire, it consumes the land; as a person, it eats its own arm. Even this, though, does not exhaust God’s wrath against sin., 21
The principle of retribution is an important biblical teaching. People reap what they sow, whether to destruction or benefit (Gal. 6:7, 8).

See note on 1:21. On social injustice, see 1:23.

**poor ... fatherless.** The object of the Lord’s special care. See 1:16–18; 11:4; Ps. 9:18 and notes.

**my people.** It is significant when the Lord identifies His people as belonging to Him. See note on 40:1.

The day of the Lord (2:11 note).

**from afar.** The desolation brought by the Assyrians.

God makes the nations serve Him as instruments of His will, but they continue to be responsible for their acts (5:25; 7:20 and notes). God’s anger is against those who administer His kingdom on earth corruptly, both rulers and people (9:12, 17, 21; 10:4, 25).
Includes Israel and Judah (v. 11).
Human rulers have their own reasons for acting, yet they end up doing exactly what the Lord has purposed from the beginning (cf. Ezek. 38:10).

Assyria conquered these cities: Calno (Calneh; cf. Amos 6:2) in 738 B.C.; Carchemish in 717 B.C.; Hamath in 738 and 720 B.C.; Arpad in 740 B.C.; Samaria in 722 B.C.; and Damascus in 732 B.C. Cf. 36:19; 37:12, 13. In each pair, the first city is further away from Assyria than the second; the boast is that Assyria will continue to extend its sphere of influence wider and wider.

Assyria boasts of its power, demonstrated in the destruction of nations with far more impressive idols than Jerusalem and Samaria (cf. Dan. 4:30; Luke 12:18–20). The irony is rich: Jerusalem and Samaria ought not to have idols at all, but should trust in the Lord. In reality, though, their trust is in idols that cannot measure up even in an idol contest.

**kingdoms.** See note on 13:4.

The Assyrian assault is itself part of God’s work.

**Zion.** Jerusalem. See note on 1:8.
A restatement of vv. 5–11. For similar expressions of pride, see 14:13, 14; Ezek. 28:2–5.
See note on v. 5. It is ridiculous for a tool to boast about its mighty accomplishments.
The Lord can destroy the tool when its usefulness is over.

A symbol of God’s blessing. See note on 2:5.

**it will burn and devour.** Cf. 9:18.

See note on 4:2. What people think should be honored or despised means little before God’s fiery judgment.

**forest ... fruitful land.** The Assyrian pride will end quickly like thorns in a fire. Little will remain (v. 19).

The day of God’s judgment. See note on 2:11.

**remnant.** The Lord will preserve a faithful few out of the destruction. See note on 1:8.

**him who struck them.** The remnant will no longer put their faith in Assyria, as Ahaz did in ch. 7.

Recalls God’s promise to Abraham (Gen. 22:17; cf. 1 Kin. 4:20). Paul cites this verse in Rom. 9:27.

**decreed.** God is determined in His judgment (v. 23; 28:22).
GOD **of hosts.** The Lord’s military title. See notes on 1:9, 24.
A word of encouragement for the remnant in Judah (37:6; 41:10, 13; 43:1). See note on 35:4.

The one to fear is not the Assyrian king, but the Lord who is bringing the Assyrians in judgment on Judah.

**destruction.** The instruments of destruction will themselves be destroyed.
Two examples are taken from the history of redemption: the defeat of Midian at the rock of Oreb (a Midianite leader; Judg. 7:25), and the victory over Egypt at the Red Sea (Ex. 14:26–28).
See 9:4. Their prosperity will be such that, like a muscular ox, the yoke will not be able to contain their neck.

Describes a march to Judah from north to south through the cities mentioned. The last, Nob, is within sight of Zion. For a similar portrayal of Assyria’s invasion, but from the southwest, see Mic. 1:10–16.
The Assyrians may inspire Judah with terror, but the Lord will intervene.

The Assyrians are portrayed as a forest that the Lord is going to cut down (v. 18 note).

**Majestic One.** See 33:21.

All that will be left of the Davidic dynasty after God’s judgment is a stump. The privileged sons of David, no less than Assyria, will be like trees that have been chopped down (10:33, 34; cf. Jer. 22:30). But in spite of this judgment on Judah, the Lord will raise up new leadership from David’s dynasty (Jer. 23:5, 6; Matt. 1:1). The remaining stump will be living, and it will send forth a shoot, a branch that will bear fruit.

**Jesse.** David’s father (1 Sam. 16:10–13). David inaugurated a great kingdom, but the greater David (Ezek. 34:23–25; Zech. 12:7–10), now only a tender plant (53:2), will rule an incomparably greater kingdom.

**branch.** See note on 4:2.

LORD**.** As the fourfold repetition emphasizes, the same God-given endowment of the Spirit that brought David his successes (1 Sam. 16:13; Ps. 51:11) will empower the Messiah (42:1; 61:1; Luke 3:22). The Spirit is the creative agent for establishing God’s kingdom (Gen. 1:2; Judg. 3:10; 6:34; 1 Sam. 10:6 and notes).

**rest upon him.** The Spirit came in a powerful way on saints in the OT to equip them for service: Moses (Num. 11:17); certain elders (Num. 11:25, 26); Joshua (Deut. 34:9); the judges (Judg. 3:10; 11:29; 13:25); kings (1 Sam. 11:6); and prophets (1 Sam. 10:10; 2 Sam. 23:2; 1 Kin. 22:24; 2 Kin. 2:15; Mic. 3:8). The Spirit is the divine agent of restoration (32:15; Joel 2:28–32).

**wisdom.** Solomon prayed for wisdom and understanding (1 Kin. 3:9), the administrative skills needed to govern the people in righteousness and justice. See Introduction to the Wisdom Literature.

**counsel.** Authoritative plans and decisions. Human counsel may or may not be in accord with God’s plan (30:1), but the Messiah’s counsel is by “the Spirit” (see 9:6).

**knowledge.** Refers to wise and submissive living in accordance with the will of God (33:6; 53:11). It is a perfection of God (40:14).

**fear of the** LORD**.** Fearing God includes obeying His commandments out of faith that the Lord will keep His threats against transgressors (Prov. 1:7 note).
See note on 2:4.

See note on 1:21.

**poor ... meek.** Those who long for divine righteousness and justice (25:4) because of oppression by the rulers of this earth (3:15; 10:2; 32:7; 61:1). They are the afflicted, oppressed, and humble whom Jesus blesses (Matt. 5:3–10; cf. Ps. 19:8 note).

**equity.** The Hb. word also means “level” or “straight” (40:4). God’s judgment is balanced and fair.

**rod ... breath.** With great power and authority (Pss. 2:9; 82:8; Rev. 6:15–17; 20:11, 12) the Messiah will conquer by His word (49:2; 61:1; Heb. 4:12; Rev. 19:15).

See note on 1:21; cf. 25:1; 33:6.

**the belt of his loins.** In antiquity, people wore long flowing robes that could be tucked into a belt in order to prepare for vigorous action (cf. Eph. 6:14).

Carnivorous animals, remade with natures that protect what they formerly devoured, effectively portray the wonderful peace on earth in the new age ruled by the Messiah (see 2:4). The devouring nations, such as Assyria, will no longer assault God’s people. The vision corresponds to reconciling love already visible in the church (Eph. 2:14–18), which will be consummated in the new heavens and new earth (Rev. 21:4, 24–27).

Mount Zion (cf. 2:2–4).

**the earth shall be full.** See Hab. 2:14.

The day of God’s judgment. See note on 2:11.

**root of Jesse.** See note on v. 1 (Rev. 22:16).

**signal.** Here, a sign of hope (cf. John 12:32), in contrast to 5:26 (see note).

**glorious.** Displaying God’s glory. See note on 4:2.

The first time God reclaimed His people from Egypt through the exodus; the second time will be from the exile (51:9–11).

**remnant.** See note on 1:8. The Lord will lead His children from wherever they are distressed.

The remnant will come from all of the known world (24:15; 42:4, 10; 51:5; 59:18, 19; cf. Matt. 24:31). The nations listed in v. 11 are located geographically on all sides of Israel and Judah: Assyria, Elam, and Shinar are to the east, in and around Mesopotamia; Egypt, Pathros, and Cush are to the south; Hamath is north, and the coastlands are to the west.

The era of restoration will witness a reconciliation of the disunited and hostile tribes. When the remnant later returns to the land after the exile, the people offer sacrifices on behalf of all twelve tribes (Ezra 6:17; 8:35).
Represent freedom from the oppression, subjugation, and harassment that had characterized Israel’s experience in the land (cf. 54:3; Mic. 5:6 note for a similar use of Assyria).

The second exodus will come by another miracle similar to the parting of the Red Sea (vv. 11, 12). However, this deliverance will be even greater, dividing the Euphrates into seven channels, not merely into two.

**scorching breath.** See Ex. 14:24–27 and Is. 11:4.

**in sandals.** The water of the great Euphrates will become so shallow that people will be able cross without even taking off their shoes.
The Lord provides an image to confirm the certainty of His salvation (19:23; 35:8, 9; 40:3–5; 57:14; 62:10). Just as He led His people out of Egypt, so He will lead them out of exile.

Isaiah’s new hymn at the second exodus corresponds to that of Moses at the first (Ex. 15).

**12:1 in that day.** The day of God’s judgment. See note on 2:11.

**I will give thanks.** The prophet speaks as a representative of the people of God. The reason for praise is God Himself.

**that you might comfort me.** Comfort is a key feature of the second half of Isaiah’s prophecy. See 40:1.

See Ex. 15:2. He is the source and the initiator of salvation (49:6, 8; 51:6, 8; 56:1; 62:1).

**the Lord God.** There is a double reference to the covenant name of God (Ex. 3:15) in the designation Lord God (Yah Yahweh). This is a poetic device to emphasize the certainty of the salvation He provides.

The salvation of the Lord always brings joy (35:10; 51:3, 11; 61:3), as God removes the causes for sorrow and anxiety.

**water ... wells.** Salvation is compared to an abundance of water (Pss. 1:3; 65:9; 104:10–13; 107:35) coming “from the wells of salvation” (41:18; cf. John 4:14).
God’s glory is a key theme in Isaiah. See 2:11, 17; 33:5.

An allusion to “triumphed gloriously” (Ex. 15:1) and a synonym for “exalted” (v. 4).

**made known in all the earth.** See 11:9.

Isaiah prophesies concerning the day of the Lord and what it means for the nations. Babylon and Assyria are treated together in the first oracle (13:1–14:27) because Babylon became the crown jewel of the Assyrian Empire and subsequently replaced it. Assyrian kings had themselves crowned as kings of this renowned city. Babylon was regarded as an epitome of religion and culture, and as such Babylon represents the kingdoms of this world. Peter and John continue to use Babylon as a symbol for ungodly nations (1 Pet. 5:13; Rev. 14:8; 16:19; 17:1–18:24).

**13:1 oracle.** The Hb. word can mean a literal weight, corresponding to the idea that the prophetic word is a heavy responsibility for the prophet who must deliver it. On the other hand, the word can also mean simply a message or oracle, without the suggestion of weight. It is often used for judgment oracles, but it can also refer to other prophetic messages.

The Lord directs the nations like a military commander. See note on 5:26.

**gates of the nobles.** Implies that the city is proud.
The armies God uses as instruments of judgment.

The great noise indicates the exercise of God’s power (30:30, 31; 33:3; Ps. 29:5–9).

**kingdoms, of nations.** The Lord is the commander of human kingdoms. In Isaiah’s era, Bab­ylon thinks of herself as “the glory of kingdoms” (13:19) or the “mistress of kingdoms” (47:5) and rules over others with great force (14:16).
