Describes the terror of the day of the Lord.

**13:6 the day of the** LORD**.** Also called “the day” (v. 13); see note on 2:11.
The people will be utterly helpless, lacking the strength to resist their enemies (Jer. 6:24; Ezek. 7:17).
The Bible often uses this imagery to convey intense pain and suffering (21:3; 49:24; 50:43; Ps. 48:6; Mic. 4:9; cf. Rom. 8:22).

Imagery for God’s cosmic judgment (24:23; Joel 2:10, 31; Matt. 24:29; Rev. 6:12–14). The Lord reigns over the entire cosmos.

**light.** See note on 2:5. The ancients worshiped the heavenly bodies, but Scripture teaches that God is the creator of them all (Deut. 4:19). Darkness symbolizes judgment. The imagery is also used for the final destruction of the world (34:3).
See note on 29:20.
Ophir produced particularly fine gold in the ancient world, gold fit for royalty and temples (see 1 Chr. 29:4; Ps. 45:9).

verse_quote: make the heavens tremble ... the earth will be shaken.
note: These expressions depict the coming of God in judgment against His creation. The shaking of the world symbolizes the overthrow of all that unbelievers exalt as rivals to God (2:12–18). The king of Babylon is described as one who makes “the earth tremble” (14:16).
The attractiveness of Bab­ylon will become a phantom when people realize how short-lived human kingdoms are.

The terrors brought by war.

**13:16 houses.** Places of safety where people keep all of their worldly possessions. See note on 24:10.

Inhabitants of the Zagros Mountains, east of Babylon and Assyria. They were never subjugated by Assyria and joined Babylon in the conquest of Assyria (612–609 B.C.). For the dating of this prophecy it is significant that Persia, which conquered Media in 549 B.C., is not mentioned.

See note on v. 4.

**Chaldeans.** Chaldea was part of Babylon and the home of the dynasty founded by Nebuchadnezzar’s father, Nabopolassar. “Chaldeans” sometimes serves as an alternative name for the Babylonians.

**Sodom and Gomorrah.** The fate of these cities is a perpetual reminder of the total destructiveness of the Lord’s judgment. See note on 1:9.
The measure of God’s judgment on human pride. Centuries after this prophecy, Babylon is finally laid waste as described.

Or owls. It is not always easy to identify the specific kind of bird in view in the OT.

**13:21, 22 wild animals ... jackals.** Babylon becomes unfit for human habitation; only wild animals haunt the site (34:11–15; Jer. 50:39; 51:37; Zeph. 2:14, 15).,

Election is God’s choice, and He is free to set Israel aside or to choose Israel again for a new future (41:8, 9; 44:1, 2; 45:4; 65:9; Ex. 19:6; Deut. 7:6; cf. Rom. 9–11). Babylon’s downfall is the necessary prerequisite for the restoration of God’s people.

**sojourners ... will attach themselves.** See Is. 56:3.
Instruments of God’s plan of redemption (55:5; 60:1–18; 61:5–7; 66:19, 20; cf. Ezra 1:1–8).

A taunt against the king of Babylon. Victors in the ancient world frequently sang taunt songs against their victims (v. 7; 12:1; Ex. 15:1).

**14:3 rest.** As in the first exodus, God will liberate the people from oppression.

The Hb. term has a range of meanings, including brief sayings like those in the book of Proverbs, and a figurative poem like the one here. The form of the song as a lament is ironic, as if the end of Babylon were a tragic death.

**king of Babylon.** A chief representative of oppressive human power.
The symbol of oppressive power is broken by God.
Instead of “the song of the ruthless” (25:5), a new song of salvation will be heard in response to God’s judgment and deliverance (24:14, 16; 26:1, 19; 44:23; 49:13). See note on 12:1–6.

Nature responds to God’s acts of judgment and restoration (55:13; 60:13; cf. 37:24). The trees may also represent the surrounding nations, which are now left to flourish in peace.

**no woodcutter.** Ancient Near Eastern kings boast in their annals of the magnificent trees they cart off from pillaged lands to build their splendid palaces.

Isaiah uses the popular conception of the realm of the dead with its shadowy figures welcoming newcomers in an ironic description of Babylon’s fall and her descent into the lower regions. The use of these conventional ideas is poetic, and is not intended as a theology of the afterlife. See 5:14 and note; Prov. 1:12; 9:18 and notes.

**14:9 thrones.** The defeated kings had thrones in their royal graves. By contrast the king of Babylon is given a bed of maggots (v. 11).

Represents in an exaggerated way the fall of Babylon, with all its imperial ambitions, into destruction (cf. Lam. 2:1; Luke 4:6; 10:15). Cf. the claims and fate of the king of Tyre in Ezek. 28.

**O Day Star, son of Dawn.** Lit. “shining one, son of dawn.” Probably refers to the planet Venus, rising in the morning and climbing toward the top of the sky, only to be overtaken by the sun. In the ancient world, observations of this astronomical cycle gave rise to several myths. Babylon seems to have thought of itself as fulfilling such a heavenly destiny and becoming an eternal and universal empire. But with the appearance of God (v. 22), Babylon’s light will be extinguished. Traditionally, this passage has also been seen as a picture of Satan’s fall from grace.

According to Canaanite myths, the god El presides over an assembly of gods on Mount Zaphon in Syria. The king of Babylon is ready to claim this exalted honor for himself.

**far reaches of the north.** A traditional rendering of Hb. _zaphon_. Ps. 48:1, 2 mentions “the far north” as belonging to the Lord alone, rather than to El or Babylon.

See Gen. 14:19, 20. This is a restatement of v. 13. People may claim rule over the entirety of God’s kingdom, but God is still sovereign. The greater their pride, the greater their fall. The conflict between nations is not part of a conflict between rival deities, as in ancient Near Eastern mythology, but an unequal battle between the Most High God and mere humans.
See vv. 9–11 and notes. Death and entry to Sheol is the ultimate proof of the emptiness of the king of Babylon’s claims to be a god (see Ezek. 28:2).
See note on 13:4.
Babylon has used the power of which it was so proud for destruction and cruelty.

The satirical contrast introduced in v. 9 is taken up again. The conquered kings are pictured in honored rest, while proud Babylon is thrown out like unhealthy refuse. To be deprived of a proper burial was regarded as a great misfortune in the ancient world.
Unlike Israel, Assyria has no remnant (v. 30; cf. 15:9; 17:3 and 1:9 note).
See note on 13:21, 22. In modern Hebrew, the word means “hedgehog,” but it is possible that in ancient Hebrew, a type of bird is meant. The same word also appears in Is. 34:11 and Zeph 2:14.

verse_quote: I will break the Assyrian in my land.
note:
The oracle shifts from distant deliverance to the more immediate threat of Assyria. The imminent demise of the Assyrian army in the days of Hezekiah will provide a lesson in the Lord’s sovereign power over history (see Is. 36; 37).

**yoke.** See note on 9:4.
These verses concluding the section that began at 13:1 are an eloquent statement of God’s irresistible hand of judgment extended over the whole earth (43:13)., 27
Prophetic message. See note on 13:1. Ahaz dies in 715 B.C., fourteen years before the siege of Jerusalem (2 Kin. 18:13).

See note on 10:5. Around the time of Ahaz’s death there is a Philistine revolt against the Assyrian emperor Sargon.

**broken.** This weakness in Assyria’s hegemony is temporary.

**adder ... flying fiery serpent.** There is no need to identify the snakes with particular kings, like Sennacherib, Esarhaddon, or Ashurbanipal. The idea is that Assyrian strength will go on for more than one generation despite successions of kings. The next generation will be more fearsome than the previous.

The object of the Lord’s special care. See 11:4; Ps. 19:8 and notes.

**remnant.** See note on v. 22.
The Assyrian invasion.

The Philistines seek to create a coalition with Judah and other nations to rebel against the Assyrians, but God’s response through Isaiah is clear. God will protect His own, in spite of the political and military turmoil, without the need for external alliances.

This oracle of judgment against Moab is probably delivered around the time of Sargon’s defeat of Moab in 715 B.C. See also 11:14; 25:10; Jer. 48; Ezek. 25:8–11; Amos 2:1–3; Zeph. 2:8–11. The oracle concerns Moab’s distress (ch. 15) and the response to Moab’s distress (ch. 16).

**15:1 oracle.** Prophetic message. See note on 13:1.

**Moab.** Moab is a nation east of the Dead Sea, between the Ammonites and the Edomites. In the ancient world, her relations with Judah are often tense.

**Ar ... Kir.** The city of Ar is on the Arnon River, and Kir is the capital of Moab.

Dibon is a site north of the Arnon River devoted to the worship of the Moabite god Chemosh. The high places are the sites of pagan worship.

**Nebo ... Medeba.** Nebo is a village north of the Arnon River, not far from the mountain where Moses went to look at the Promised Land (Deut. 34:1). Medeba is five miles (8 km) to the southeast.

**baldness.** The customs of mourning include cutting the hair and shaving.

In the public places, where people gather.

**sackcloth ... tears.** Mourning customs (v. 2; 22:12; Jer. 4:8; 41:5; 48:20, 34; Lam. 2:10).

These two towns are close together, about six miles (10 km) north of Medeba (v. 2). Heshbon was captured by Israel under Moses (Num. 21:23–26).

**Jahaz.** Located on the Arnon River, about twenty miles (32 km) south of Heshbon (Num. 21:23; Jer. 48:34).

Isaiah has noticeably more sympathy for Moab, Ruth’s homeland (16:11), than for the other nations.

**Zoar.** The Moabites flee to Zoar, as their forefather Lot had done (Gen. 19:23–30). Their escape route appears to go south, away from the invaders coming from the north.

**Luhith ... Horonaim.** Unidentified cities probably close to Zoar (Jer. 48:3, 5, 34).
Possibly a seasonal stream southeast of the Dead Sea (Jer. 48:34).
Possibly the Zered River on the border between Moab and Edom (v. 8).

A city on the Arnon River.

**a lion.** The fugitives go from trouble to trouble (cf. Amos 5:19) in their flight southward. They finally turn to Judah in the west for asylum (16:1–5).

The Moabites are shepherds (Num. 32:3, 4), and can send lambs as tokens of their submission (cf. 2 Kin. 3:4).

**from Sela.** The fugitives are either at Sela, a naturally fortified site in Edom or at a mountain stronghold (Hb. _sela_ means “rock,” or “cliff”). The tribute is sent from their outpost to Judah.

**Zion.** See note on 1:8.
The fugitives became refugees fleeing to the south (15:8, 9).
The prophet requests protection from the heat of the day.
Assyria.

God made a covenant with David (55:3; 2 Sam. 22:51; Ps. 89:28; see 54:8). In Jesus, the Son of David, the nations find shelter (Acts 15:16, 17).

**throne ... tent of David.** Hope lies in the Lord and in His promises to David (9:2–7; 11:1–9; Amos 9:11, 12).
A delicacy associated with celebrations generally, and with pagan worship particularly (Hos. 3:1).

These places are not far apart (15:4; Jer. 48:32).

**vine.** The imagery of the vineyard is applied here to Moab (cf. 5:1–7).

**Jazer ... the sea.** Jazer is the extreme north of Moabite territory.

Isaiah is moved by the desolation of the fine vineyards for which Moab is well known.

**Elealeh.** See 15:4.
Trampling the grapes is generally a time of great celebration (see Jer. 25:30).

verse_quote: my inner parts moan ... my inmost self.
note: Describes deeply felt sorrow (v. 9; 21:3, 4; cf. Jer. 48:36). See note on 15:5.
Often the sites of pagan sanctuaries.
This summary regarding Moab’s distress is in prose form. Either it is a revelation in the past or a reference to the oracles in 15:1–9 or 15:1–16:12.

The desolation of Moab is at hand. Perhaps this is a reference to the quelling of the rebellion against Sargon, king of Assyria, around 715 B.C.

**like the years of a hired worker.** Impatiently.

**glory.** The prophetic word applies to all who exalt themselves and trouble the people of God. Salvation is in the Messiah (v. 5), but those who seek refuge for political or economic reasons will not find shelter in Zion.

This oracle of judgment concerning Damascus may be dated to the Syro-Ephraimite crisis of 734–732 B.C.

**17:1 oracle.** Prophetic message. See note on 13:1.

**Damascus.** Besides being the capital of Syria, it is also the commercial hub along the trade routes between Mesopotamia, Egypt, and Arabia. Damascus is captured by Tiglath-pileser III in 732 B.C.
This city is located on the Arnon River (2 Kin. 10:32, 33). Syria’s political control extends at times to the Arnon.

The “strong cities” (v. 9) of Israel are already weakened by 732 B.C. (9:1 note) and cease to exist in 722 B.C. The northern kingdom of Israel has allied itself with Syria against Judah (see 7:5, 6).

**remnant.** Unlike Israel, Syria has no remnant.

**like the glory of the children of Israel.** Normally, this would be a good thing. However, the following verses make plain that their former glory has been brought low.
A lush valley southwest of Jerusalem, it is the gateway to the western plains (Josh. 15:8; 18:16; 2 Sam. 5:18, 22; 1 Chr. 14:9).
Olive trees are beaten with sticks to shake loose the ripe fruit. Only a few olives on the topmost branches remain out of reach of the long staves.

The faithful remnant look to their Creator. The promise seems broader and more inclusive than one made simply to Israel, especially in a context relating judgment upon the nations (see 2:2–4).

**Maker.** The prophet contrasts the works of God with those of His creatures. See note on 2:8.

The Canaanite goddess Asherah is a fertility goddess, symbolized by sacred groves and poles (27:9; Ex. 34:13; Deut. 16:21; Judg. 2:13). Incense altars are also often used in pagan worship (see Ezek. 6:6).

Describes apostasy (Deut. 4:9, 23; 8:11, 14, 19; 32:18). It is not simply a description of mental states but of actions that flow from those thoughts.

**Rock.** See 8:14, 15; 26:4; Deut. 32:4.

**refuge.** The Lord alone is the strength of His people (25:4; 27:5), in contrast to military and political solutions (v. 9; 23:11, 14; 30:2).

**the vine-branch of a stranger.** Israel has worked diligently to cultivate relationships and alliances with her neighbors, as a farmer might cultivate an exotic seedling. Yet in the process they have forgotten the Lord, who is the nation’s true refuge. As a result, all of this hard work will come to nothing.

Perhaps this alludes to a pagan practice in which potted plants are forced to sprout in order to secure fertile crops.

**harvest.** The end will bring nothing but disaster.

verse_quote: thundering of the sea ... mighty waters.
note: The destructive power of the nations appears to be like that of the “seas” and “mighty waters” (8:7 note). In ancient Near Eastern myths, the sea represents chaos and death (Ezek. 28:2; 32:2 and notes). Yet the Lord is the one who truly thunders with power (Ezek. 1:24): when He acts, the seemingly-powerful nations are blown away before Him like chaff (see Ps. 1:4).

To be driven away as chaff (cf. 29:5; 41:15, 16; Ps. 83:13) reveals a lack of life, value, and stability.

**mountains.** In Isaiah’s day, grain is winnowed on windy hilltops.

An unforeseen series of troubles (24:17, 18) appears on the day of the Lord’s wrath (22:5). The Lord still protects His people. He is “God with us” (8:10 note) who repays the nations for the evil done to His people. Yet none of this precludes the suffering of His people: on the contrary, the nations will only be crushed _after_ they plunder Judah.

A cry of woe. See note on 1:4.

**land of whirring wings.** This may mean either a land of “many insects” or “many ships” (so ancient translations). Lush lands are known for the quantity of their insect life. The frantic buzzing of the insects provides an image of the desperate diplomacy presented in these verses.

**Cush.** The biblical Ethiopia is the remote region of southern Egypt and beyond, including Nubia, south of the fourth cataract of the Nile. The Nubian Shabako ruled over lower Egypt from 715 B.C. (twenty-fifth dynasty). His administration tried to extend his influence northward into the delta region.

Papyrus boats that the Nubians can use to send messengers to incite the nations to rebel against Assyria.

**a nation tall and smooth.** Possibly refers to the impressive appearance of the nation or nations that the remote Nubians are trying to stir up. The specific nation is not identified, perhaps because the general hubbub of international diplomacy is in view here.

Those addressed in this oracle will observe what the Lord is doing.

**signal.** See note on 5:26. Trumpets are also commonly used as signals in war during this era. The Lord is the one who gives the signal to begin this conflict.

The Lord patiently observes the rebellion of the nations (Ps. 2:1–4).

**clear heat ... cloud of dew.** Expressive of the silent stillness as God waits to act, in contrast to the buzzing but fruitless activity of the nations (see 25:5).

These verses contain two images of God’s judgment. First, there is the pruning of the vines before harvest to encourage the development of the grapes, “shoots,” and “branches.” Second, there is the carcass on which the “birds of prey” and the wild animals feed (cf. 31:5). For a body to be left unburied as food for the wild animals and birds is a sign of judgment.

**18:6 summer ... winter.** The length of time implied emphasizes how extensive the carnage will be.

The nations offer tokens of submission to the Lord (13:4 note; 16:1 note).

**tall and smooth.** See v. 2 and note.

**the place.** The temple is the OT sign of God’s presence and reign (Deut. 12:5, 11).

An oracle of judgment concerning Egypt. In contrast to ch. 20, the language of ch. 19 is symbolic, not historically specific.

**19:1 oracle.** Prophetic message. See note on 13:1.

**the LORD is riding on a swift cloud.** An ancient Near Eastern image of deity. The cloud forms the Lord’s chariot-throne (see Pss. 18:10; 68:33).

**the idols of Egypt will tremble.** The exodus represented the Lord’s earlier victory over the gods of Egypt (Ex. 12:12).

verse_quote: I will stir up Egyptians against Egyptians.
note: Egypt spends much of the eighth century B.C. in civil war.
On idolatry and divination, see 2:6, 8; 8:19 and notes.

Egypt, too, will be subjugated; perhaps this is an allusion to Pharaoh’s cruelty before the exodus (Ex. 6:9).

**Lord** GOD **of hosts.** See note on 1:9.

This spells economic disaster for a country whose life depends on the Nile. God can easily dry up Egypt’s many waters (see Ezek. 30:12). This is also a direct assault on Pharaoh’s claim, as a god, to regulate the flow of the Nile.
In the ancient world, Egypt served as the breadbasket of many countries because of the regular flooding of the Nile (Gen. 41:57).
God’s judgment against Egypt falls on the important industries of fishing (v. 8) and flax products, for which ancient Egypt was famous.

The meaning of this Hb. word is uncertain. Some believe it is a metaphor for the nobles as the “foundation” of the society in contrast to those “who work for pay.” Others suggest “weavers” of cloth. The point is that all aspects of the society will suffer greatly.

Also known as Tanis, this is a city in the Nile Delta (Num. 13:22; Ps. 78:12, 43) and Egypt’s capital at the time.

**foolish.** God turns the wisdom of the wise into folly.

**counselors ... stupid counsel.** In contrast to the wise and effective counsel of the coming Branch; see 11:2.

**son of the wise, a son of ancient kings.** This sarcastic remark taunts Egypt’s claim to wisdom (cf. 1 Kin. 4:29–31).

verse_quote: Where then are your wise men.
note: These words addressed to Pharaoh continue to stand as a polemic against human pride (1 Cor. 1:20).

These include political, economic, and religious leaders.

**Memphis.** This city in Lower Egypt is its ancient capital.
Judgment is frequently compared to drunkenness in the OT (Is. 51:21–23; Jer. 25:15, 16): a state of staggering and confusion that ends with vomiting, falling down, and being unable to get up.
Judgment will extend from the civil and religious leaders down to the bottom of society. See 9:14, 15.
For the hand of the Lord’s judgment, see 14:26, 27.

verse_quote: the land of Judah will become a terror to the Egyptians.
note: Given the difference in their relative sizes, this is a remarkable prophecy. This will remove the temptation for Judah to seek military alliances with the Egyptians.

Not just one but five cities will turn to the Lord.

**language of Canaan.** Shows how great a change is in view, because anything Canaanite is an abomination to the ancient Egyptians (Gen. 43:32; 46:34).

**swear allegiance to the** LORD**.** Submit completely to God.

**City of Destruction.** Probably refers to Heliopolis (“City of the Sun”; see text note). Jewish scribes parodied the name by changing the Hb. word for “sun” to the almost identical Hb. word for “destruction.”

The altar (v. 19) signifies their commitment to the Lord (cf. Gen. 12:8; 28:22; Josh. 22:26–29), while the pillar will be a memorial commemorating God’s great work (cf. Gen. 28:18–22).

**savior and defender.** As in the days of the judges, God will fill these roles to deliver His people from oppressors (Judg. 2:18; 3:9, 15).
Divine discipline will draw the Egyptians to the Lord (30:26; Hos. 6:1; 14:1, 2, 4). If He can do these things for the Egyptians, how much more will He do for His own people?

Building this link between Egypt and Assyria symbolizes the removal of the alienation between them (cf. 11:16 note).

**Egypt to Assyria.** These two great cultures find unity in a common commitment to the Lord. Since they are at opposite ends of ancient Israel’s universe (Assyria in the north, Egypt in the south), the implication is that all of the other nations of the world will likewise be included in this hope-filled future.

verse_quote: blessing in the midst of the earth.
note: Israel, Egypt, and Assyria will join in the patriarchal promises (Gen. 12:2, 3).

verse_quote: people ... work of my hands ... inheritance.
note: Each will share in full covenant membership, signified by three designations: “people” (cf. 10:24; 40:1 note; Ps. 100:3; Jer. 11:4; Hos. 2:23); “work of my hands” (60:21; Pss. 119:73; 138:8); “inheritance” (cf. Deut. 32:9).

Sargon II, king of Assyria from 722 to 705 B.C.

**Ashdod.** This Philistine city rebels against Assyria at the encouragement of Shabako, the Nubian king (18:1 note) in 713 B.C. It falls in 711 B.C. An inscription mentioning Sargon by name has been unearthed at Ashdod. The lack of Egyptian help for her former allies serves as a potent lesson to all of the folly of relying on Egypt.

The Lord orders Isaiah to be partially clad like a prisoner of war going into exile. Sackcloth is a garment for times of mourning (15:3; 22:12; 37:1, 2; 58:5) and a distinctive prophetic garment (2 Kin. 1:8; Zech. 13:4). Several prophets perform similar kinds of sign-acts, designed to display their message in pictorial form, especially when their audience is hostile or unreceptive (cf. Ezek. 4).

Refers to a position of trust and honor before God. Moses was God’s friend and servant (Ex. 14:31; Num. 12:7, 8; Deut. 34:5). Abraham (Ps. 105:42); Jacob (Ezek. 28:25); Joshua (Josh. 24:29); David (37:35; 2 Sam. 3:18; Ps. 132:10); the Suffering Servant (52:13–53:12); and groups of people such as the prophets (44:26) and restored Israel (41:8, 9; 43:10; 44:1, 2, 21; 45:4; 48:20) are also reckoned as the Lord’s servants. God’s servants may suffer, but they are promised a great heritage as servants of the Lord (54:17; 65:8, 9, 13–15; 66:14).

**three years.** It could designate the time that Isaiah walks about as a sign or the duration before the sign will be realized.

**sign and a portent.** The prophetic style of life (8:18; cf. Deut. 13:1, 2; Jer. 32:20) demonstrates the folly of relying on Egypt, for Egypt, like any nation, is vulnerable.
Esarhaddon fulfills this prophecy in 671 B.C.

Ashdod is one of the Philistine cities on the coastal plain.

**in that day.** The day of judgment. See note on 2:11.

**in whom we hoped.** Egypt’s fate will persuade the people that no ally can help them escape.

Prophetic message. See note on 13:1.

**wilderness of the sea.** This is probably a sarcastic parody. Babylon’s southern region on the Persian Gulf, known as “Land of the Sea,” will become a wilderness or as good as a wilderness to anyone looking for salvation from there. Neither the wilderness nor the sea is able to sustain life.

The prophet is overwhelmed by what he sees.

**betrays ... destroys.** In the course of waging war, nations change sides and break former alliances.

**Elam ... Media.** Elam is a major region of Persia and allies itself with Media in 700 B.C. Perhaps as a part of Assyria’s army (5:26 note), Elam helps to conquer Babylon in 689 B.C. But Elam and her allies certainly conquer Babylon in 539 B.C. (11:11; 13:17 and notes).

**the sighing.** Could refer to the groan of Babylon under Assyrian domination or to the groan of the nations under Babylonian control. The former is more likely because Babylon does not again become dominant in the region until 605 B.C.

The expressions in these verses convey great psychological suffering on the prophet’s part (16:9–11; 22:4; cf. Dan. 8:27; 10:16, 17). The report of Babylon’s fall may distress Isaiah because now no one can rescue Judah from Assyria. The image of a woman in labor is a common one in the prophets for extreme pain and anguish., 4
Prepare for battle.
Isaiah is God’s watchman in Judah.
Probably signs of an approaching army.

Finally, the seductive power of Babylon, her religion (17:7–9; 27:9; 46:1–13), and her culture have come to an end (13:19). See Rev. 14:8; 18:2.

**all the carved images of her gods.** Not only has Babylon been defeated but her gods as well (cf. 19:1).
Judah is portrayed as an oppressed people, much like the grain under the threshing sledge (28:27, 28; 41:15, 16; Amos 1:3). See note on 40:1.

Prophetic message. See note on 13:1.

**Dumah.** An oasis in Edom at the intersection of the roads from the Red Sea to Palmyra and from the Persian Gulf to Petra. The name means “silence” or “stillness” in Hebrew, representing the future of the once bustling land of Edom.

**Seir.** A significant mountain in Edom, which represents the whole land (cf. Ezek. 35). The Edomites ask the prophet what the future will hold.

The future holds both hope and judgment, specifically, relief from Assyrian domination followed by oppression from Babylon. However, the vagueness of the response implies that deliverance may yet be a long time in coming.

Prophetic message. See note on 13:1.

**concerning Arabia.** In Hebrew this sounds like “at evening.”

**Dedanites.** Dedan is an oasis two hundred miles (320 km) south of Dumah (Ezek. 27:20; 38:13). For safety, they will pass the night in the thickets rather than in more conventional lodging places.

An oasis located ninety miles (145 km) north of Dedan (Jer. 25:23). The desert peoples provide food and water for the fugitives from the battle. The fact that fugitives appear in these remote locations is a sign of how intense the battle will be.

Arabia’s glory will be directly affected by what happens in Babylon.

**according to the years of a hired worker.** See note on 16:14.

**Kedar.** Arabia, including Syria; the area inhabited by Bedouin tribes (Jer. 49:28, 29).

An oracle of judgment concerning the Valley of Vision, Jerusalem. The placement of an oracle concerning Jerusalem in the midst of oracles against foreign nations may be explained by the historical association of Jerusalem with Babylon. Jerusalem trusted in Babylon during the Assyrian hegemony, but ultimately was taken into captivity by her former ally. The occasion for this particular oracle may be Ashdod’s rebellion and the Assyrian campaign in 711 B.C., or the lifting of the siege on Jerusalem after the devastation of Judah in 701 B.C. Much of it looks back on past events.

**22:1 oracle.** Prophetic message. See note on 13:1.

**valley of vision.** May be intended as an insult, to the effect that the city built on a hill (2:1) is now a valley, and though they think they can see, they are actually blind.

**to the housetops.** The Assyrians having left, the people gather on the housetops for purposes of socializing and celebrating (v. 13).

The noisy and excited citizenry has not seen what the prophet has seen. They have become complacent (32:13; Zeph. 2:15; 3:11).

**not slain with the sword.** They have run away (v. 3).

The people were once governed by unreliable and selfish leaders who now have abandoned them to save their own lives (2 Kin. 25:4–6). The prophet is critical of human leadership and of people who have no understanding of what is happening around them (1:23–26; 3:13–15; 9:14–17; 19:13–15; 28:7–13; 29:15).

verse_quote: do not labor to comfort me.

This section is often called an “apocalypse,” which is a genre in which something hidden is revealed, often filled with symbolism and having to do with cataclysm and judgment. The prophet holds before sinners and godly people the clear teaching that the day of the Lord brings judgment on creation and the fullness of salvation for the saints. God’s plan of redemption includes restoration from exile, the blessings of Christ in the church, and the establishment of God’s kingdom in all nations. Chapter 24 focuses on God’s overthrow of the corrupted earth; ch. 25, on the praise that comes to Him in response; and chs. 26 and 27 on God’s interaction with His people. Brilliant assonances, impossible to translate, enhance the prophetic message.

This historical bridge between chs. 1–35 and 40–66 directly parallels 2 Kin. 18:13–20:19. It records the fulfillment of Isaiah’s predictions that the Lord would judge Judah by bringing the Assyrian army to the gates of Jerusalem and would then judge that proud army by destroying it there, preserving a faithful remnant in the city. Hezekiah’s faith contrasts with the response of his father, Ahaz, to the prophetic word. Hezekiah by faith accepts a sign when confronted with illness (38:7, 8); Ahaz refused to ask for a sign (7:12). Yet even Hezekiah falls into the same temptation to trust in the nations as his forefathers did, seeking to impress the envoys from Babylon with his resources (ch. 39). The result is the inevitability of exile. Thus, the first two chapters of the bridge (36; 37) deal with the main subject of the first half of the book of Isaiah—Assyria—while chs. 38; 39 transition to the subject of the second half of the book—Babylon. Because of this concern, the events seem to be presented out of chronological order: before Sennacherib moved west to attack Judah, he had already defeated Merodach-baladan and the Babylonians, so Merodach-baladan would have had no reason to seek an alliance with Judah. Isaiah arranges his material thematically, placing the visit of Merodach-baladan after the defeat of Assyria even though the visit happened before Assyria’s defeat at the hands of the angel of the Lord (37:36–38).

**36:1 fourteenth year.** The precise chronology of the reigns of Hezekiah and his father, Ahaz, is difficult to determine, and scholars disagree on the dating (Introduction to 1 Kings: Chronology; 2 Kings 16:1 note). These notes assume that Hez­ekiah rules alongside Ahaz as co-regent from c. 727–c. 715 B.C. and is sole king from c. 715–c. 696 B.C. (2 Kin. 18:1, 2 and notes). While some explain the “fourteenth” year as a copyist’s error for “twenty-fourth,” it is more probable that Isaiah is referring to the beginning of Hezekiah’s independent rule in 715 B.C., which would make 701 B.C. the king’s fourteenth year as the sole ruler of Judah.

Isaiah originally addressed these words to the future exiles in Babylon to encourage them to flee from there and return by faith to the Promised Land (e.g., 48:20, 21). The encouragement partially arises from the supernatural character of his words (e.g., 41:21–27). These prophecies, originally delivered more than a century and a half before the end of the exile (see Introduction: History of Interpretation), astonish their audience by predicting Israel’s (i.e., Judah’s) immediate deliverance from Babylon by Cyrus (e.g., 44:24–45:13), the coming of the suffering Christ to save them from their sins after they return to the land (42:1–7; 49:1–13; 50:4–11; 52:13–53:12), and Israel’s final salvation in the last days (51:6). The near, more remote, and most remote prophecies merge together on the canvas. From Isaiah’s perspective, the restoration after the exile inaugurates the new age, and this first taste of salvation through God’s servant, Cyrus, coalesces with the greater salvation that the Christ, God’s Servant, will bring His people. Today, the elect have even more confidence in these words of prophecy because they have been fulfilled in Christ and are being fulfilled in His church (2 Pet. 1:19). These chapters lay the foundation for Isaiah’s theme of a new exodus. Numerous passages in this section of Isaiah (40:3–11; 41:17–20; 42:14–17; 43:16–21; 44:1–5, 27; 48:20, 21; 49:8–12; 50:2; 51:9, 10; 52:11, 12; 55:12, 13) develop a paradigm to demonstrate that the exodus theme has become “eschatologized.” That is, the exodus imagery has developed now into the expectation of a promised future event, which is developed on the basis of God’s past action in delivering His people. Isaiah is teaching that the foundational salvific event in Israel’s history now becomes a paradigm for a new salvation event that will be far more significant than even the epochal deliverance of the Israelites from Egypt.

**what is to happen ... outcome.** The Lord alone plans, declares, and executes. See note on 11:2.

**former things.** See 42:9; 43:9; 46:9; 48:3. These include past prophecies of events, especially God’s abandonment of Israel and Judah as recorded in chs. 1–35. They might also include the Lord’s earlier acts of salvation. Fulfilled prophecy is a key evidence of the Lord’s existence and power.

**things to come.** See 42:23; 44:7; 45:11; 46:10. These are prophecies of the Lord’s favor and the full establishment of His kingdom, as in chs. 40–66.
God taunts the pagan gods for their complete inability to act in any direction. They have no power to terrify anyone, unlike the Lord.
God condemns those who turn away from Him.

The Lord shows His sovereignty over the nations.

**north ... rising of the sun.** Cyrus came from Persia in the east and conquered Media in 550 B.C., becoming master of territories north of Babylon. He executed the Lord’s will (45:4, 5; 2 Chr. 36:23; Ezra 1:1–4). From an Israelite and Judean perspective, he also came from the north, as nations outside of that region came into the fertile crescent from the north when they were executing campaigns in the area.

**he shall call on my name.** Although Cyrus was not a believer, he acknowledged the existence of the gods of subject nations in his decree. In this case, his words were truer than he knew.

**potter.** See note on 27:11.

Probably refers to Isaiah (40:1 note).

**good news.** The gospel of God’s grace (40:9 note). In this case, the specific news of their deliverance from exile in Babylon under Cyrus, which Isaiah had declared long ago.
The nations and their idols are impotent. The Lord needs no one to advise Him for He has all wisdom in Himself.
The Lord’s assessment of idols is that they are empty, worthless (40:18–20; 41:7, 21–24; 44:9).

This is the first of four “Servant Songs” in chs. 40–55 celebrating the Servant of the Lord (49:1–7; 50:4–11; 52:13–53:12; cf. ch. 61).

**42:1 Behold.** The third in a sequence. See 41:24, 29. The idols and the nations are nothing: the alternative is found in “my Servant.”

**my servant.** See note on 20:3. Isaiah has already identified the covenant people Israel as the Servant of the Lord (41:9; cf. 42:19; 43:10; 44:2; 45:4; 48:20). Now he introduces another application of the expression to describe an individual who, by divine empowerment, stands in contrast to the ineffective nullities of idolatry (41:24, 29). This individual will succeed where Israel has failed in her divinely allotted mission. Furthermore, as the supreme embodiment of Israel, he is able to provide the salvation that the nation needs. Isaiah’s focus on this individual becomes clearer throughout the following chapters, culminating in the prophecy of 52:13–53:12.

The impact of the Servant’s ministry is not confined to Israel, but also embraces the nations. He brings justice and light to the nations, and so accomplishes what Isaiah earlier attributed to the Messiah (42:1, cf. 11:2–4; 49:6, cf. 9:2–6), with whom he is to be identified. Unlike Israel, which has been disobedient and has suffered for her own sins while nonetheless complaining of being abandoned by the Lord (40:27; 49:14), this prophetic figure is obedient, suffering in silence for Israel’s sins and looking forward in hope to final vindication. Ultimately, the servant imagery is fulfilled in Jesus (Matt. 12:15–21). But just as Isaiah envisaged a servant role for the people after the Servant completes his task (54:17; 56:6; 65:8, 9; 66:14), those who acknowledge Christ as their Savior are called on to emulate his example of servanthood (1 Pet. 2:21–25).

**uphold.** See note on 41:10. The Servant’s strength does not come from Himself but from God (cf. 40:30, 31).

**chosen.** See note on 14:1.

**delights.** The Servant pleases God and is an object of His love and favor (60:10; 62:4; Matt. 3:17; Mark 1:11; Luke 9:35). The Lord is able to use other servants, such as Cyrus (45:1), in whom He takes no such pleasure.

**justice to the nations.** God institutes His universal kingdom of justice and righteousness. “Justice” is emphatically repeated three times in vv. 1–4.
The Servant does not clamor for attention but speaks in a spirit of gentleness and patience.

This metaphor is appropriate for the poor and needy (Ps. 9:18 note). Ancient kings boasted about their ferocity and the way in which they brought subject nations to their knees. Rather than break the weak, however, the Servant will heal them.

**burning wick.** Represents people who are close to losing faith and hope.

The Servant will practice godliness on earth (cf. 2:2–4). He will be greater than Moses (Deut. 18:15–18; Acts 3:22–26), mediating a new covenant that enables people to keep His law (v. 6; 2 Cor. 3:3; Heb. 8:7–13). For the coastlands, see note on 41:1.

**wait.** See note on 8:17.

God the creator is above all creation because He made everything (4:5 note). The God who created everything has the power to fulfill His promises.

**breath ... spirit.** The Creator and Sustainer of life (Ps. 104:30; Acts 17:24, 25) will enable the Servant to transform the earth with new, spiritual life.

These expressions parallel “chosen” and “uphold,” respectively, in v. 1.

**covenant for the people.** Jesus Christ, as God’s Servant, brings the new covenant to His people (see 53:4–6; Jer. 31:31–34; Heb. 8:6–13; 9:15). This new covenant (Jer. 31:31) is also called the “covenant of peace” (54:10) and the “everlasting covenant” (55:3; 61:8).

**light for the nations.** The recipients of God’s light are a new community of light-bearers in a dark world (9:2; 49:6; 51:4; 60:1–3; Luke 2:30–32; Acts 26:17, 18, 23).

The Babylonian exile is described as a kind of dark prison. Israel’s salvation from exile prefigures a spiritual deliverance through Christ from the blindness, bondage, and darkness of sin (5:30; 29:18; 51:14 and notes). Blindness is a theme in this chapter (see v. 16, 18, 19)

Include the judgments prophesied against Damascus, Samaria, Nineveh, and Judah, as well as the Lord’s deliverance of His people from Egypt (41:22 note).

**new things.** Include renewal of the covenant, restoration to the land, the messianic kingdom, inclusion of the Gentiles, and the new heaven and earth (41:22 note).

**declare ... tell.** God plans, proclaims, and executes. His word will come to pass (11:2 note; 40:8). Unlike the idols of the nations, the Lord both speaks and does.

Represents the specific praise that the redeemed sing in response to a specific new act of deliverance, just as Moses and Miriam sang a new song after they witnessed God’s acts of salvation (Ex. 15:1, 21; cf. Is. 12:1–6 and notes; Ps. 149:1; Rev. 5:9; 14:3).

**end of the earth.** Wherever God’s children may be found (11:12), including the former Gentiles.

See note on 21:16 (60:7; Ps. 120:5; Jer. 2:10; 49:28, 29).

**Sela.** See note on 16:1. These, too, are Gentile areas that will join in singing the Lord’s praises.
The Lord receives acclamation from His subjects (v. 8; 24:14–16 note; 1 Pet. 2:9).

Assurance comes from knowing that when the Lord’s zeal is stirred, He will accomplish His plan (9:7 note).

**mighty man ... man of war.** Isaiah describes the Lord as the Divine Warrior in whom hope lies (1:9; 5:26 and notes). See note on Dan. 9:27.

**cries out.** The Hb. word here is different from the one in v. 2. This is a battle cry or call to arms, not a cry of distress.

God promises to be with His people and lead them, as He did Israel in the wilderness (Ex. 13:21, 22).

**darkness ... into light.** See 9:2.

**rough places into level ground.** See 40:4. No obstacles, whether within His people (their blindness) or external challenges, can prevent the Lord’s plan from being put into effect.
They are “deaf” because they have not listened (v. 23), and “blind” because they have refused to see the hand of God in their history (v. 20; 48:3–6).

See note on 42:1. The Lord exclaims at the blindness and deafness of Israel, who has been as weak spiritually as her neighbors. Those who are supposed to be the light to the nations are unfit for the task. In order to redeem His people, the Lord Himself will have to take the form of a servant and embrace His people’s weakness (see Phil. 2:8–11).
There is nothing wrong with God’s law: it is holy, righteous, and glorious. Yet given Israel’s failure to keep it, it became a curse rather than a blessing to His people (see Rom. 7:12, 13).
These conditions have come about because they have rebelled against the law of the Lord (v. 24).
See note on 41:8.

God in effect fought against His own people through the Assyrian and Babylonian devastation of Samaria and Judah. Yet even this act of judgment has not changed them; the law and its curse are ultimately powerless to change hard hearts.

God will establish a new and transformed community.

**43:1 created.** See note on 4:5.

**formed.** God is Israel’s creator as well as her redeemer. See note on 27:10, 11.

**Fear not.** The Lord will deliver His people. See note on 10:24; 35:4.

**redeemed.** See note on 35:8, 9.

**called ... name.** The Lord has called them to be His people and He knows them by name—an expression of His personal care for them (cf. 45:3; 49:1; 62:2; John 10:3; Rev. 2:17). The basic blessing of God’s covenant is expressed in Jer. 30:22: “You shall be my people, and I will be your God.” See also Ex. 6:7; Lev. 11:45; Jer. 11:4.

These words describe the affliction through which God will bring His people to safety (Ps. 66:6, 12). Water and fire are opposite dangers, and so they encompass every danger in between. Passing through the waters recalls the exodus from Egypt (Ex. 14), while fire often represents the Babylonian exile (29:6). Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego were literally protected from the fire (see Dan. 3, esp. v. 27).

Seba is probably South Arabia, or Eritrea. For Cush, see note on Ps. 68:31. The Lord connects the idea of redeeming His people with a concrete ransom, in this case the wealth of several nations combined.

God’s people are exalted by election (49:5; Ex. 19:5; Deut. 7:6–8). In spite of their repeated sin and rebellion against Him, for which they have been judged, the nation still belongs to the Lord, and He will not let them go.

–**7 east ... west ... north ... south ... everyone.** The Lord will bring His people back from the four points of the compass to which they have been scattered. In spite of their sin, they are still His beloved children.
Here again is the community of rebels. See notes on 29:18; 42:18, 19. Spiritually “blind” and “deaf” Israel fulfills the Lord’s prophecies in spite of her sin.

The whole world is called to the Lord’s courtroom to hear His vindication of Himself as He demonstrates that He alone is able to predict the future before it happens. In this case, He demonstrates His power through the redemption and return of His own people.

**former things.** God’s earlier prophecies. See note on 41:22.

OT Israel partially fulfilled this mandate as they returned from exile. Yet it is more completely fulfilled under the new covenant as the church, the new Israel, is commissioned to be witnesses, bringing the good news to all nations (Acts 1:8).

**servant.** See notes on 20:3; 41:8; 42:1.

verse_quote: besides me there is no savior.
note: Is. 40–48stresses the powerlessness of the idols that have surround the Jews in exile in Babylon. Here, the Lord goes further to declare their nonexistence. The idols of the nations don’t merely do nothing; they are nothing.

The Lord alone from old willed the redemption of His people (40:21; 41:4).

**deliver from my hand.** See Deut. 32:39. The Lord’s power to judge is what proves His power to deliver His own people.

See 35:9; 41:14 and notes.

**Babylon** . The Lord’s deliverance specifically includes Babylon as the place from which His people will be delivered long before they are exiled there. The oracles in Is. 40–66, though originally addressed to the postexilic community, were revealed before the exile (cf. 40:1–55:13; 56:1–66:24 notes).

**Chaldeans.** The Babylonians. See note on 13:19.
Isaiah refers to the crossing of the Red Sea (Ex. 14; 15).

verse_quote: chariot and horse, army and warrior.
note: The prophet recalls the chariots of Egypt that were destroyed before the face of the Lord, proving the assertion made in v. 13 (cf. 31:1).

In comparison to the return from Babylon, even the exodus from Egypt will seem relatively unimportant (42:9 note). God’s action in the past has become the basis for understanding a future event. See note on 40:1–55:13.

**wilderness ... desert.** See note on 40:3.

**rivers.** See note on 41:18.

Creatures associated with desolate areas (34:11–15). See note on 13:20–22.

**water.** Recalls God’s provision in the wilderness during the first exodus (Ex. 15:22–26; 17:5, 6). See note on 1:30.

**my chosen people.** See notes on vv. 1, 3.
Instead of presenting offerings and sacrifices in response to the Lord’s great grace to them, the people were hardened in their sins and finally went into exile.

verse_quote: have not brought me your sheep.
note: The people followed more than one religious practice, but these were not necessarily offered to God. They were weary of serving Him, even though His demands on them were not burdensome. However, they had both burdened and wearied the Lord with their many sins (v. 24), and were finally exiled from the Promised Land. On the emptiness of sacrifices which are mere external rituals, see note on Jer. 7:21–23.
An aromatic plant, possibly sugarcane.

A repetition for emphasis.

**blots ... remember.** God forgives sin, as Israel experienced after the incident of the golden calf (Ex. 34:6, 7; cf. Luke 5:21). The Lord graciously promises to forgive and to establish His word (37:35; 42:21; 48:9, 11).
They stand condemned, unable to refute God’s charge. Cf. 1:18.

Jacob was the father of the twelve tribes (Hos. 12:2, 3).

**mediators.** The religious leaders, including prophets and priests.
Judah has been disgraced by the destruction of the temple and the exile of her people, because it was a divine judgment upon their many sins (63:18; cf. 2 Kin. 25:18–21).

See notes on 20:3; 41:8; 42:1.

**chosen.** See notes on 14:1; 43:3.

See note on 27:11.

**from the womb.** God likens Himself to a mother who has conceived and will give birth (v. 24; 42:14; 66:9).

**Fear not.** See notes on 10:24; 35:4.

**Jeshurun.** A poetic name for Israel meaning “upright one” (cf. Deut. 32:15).

This passage develops the promises in 28:6; 32:15. The Spirit lives in the children of the covenant today (Ezek. 36:26, 27; Joel 2:28, 29; Acts 2:38, 39).

**blessing on your descendants.** The Spirit will also confirm God’s promises. For the connection between water and the Spirit, see Mark 1:8–10. The blessings of forgiveness and the Holy Spirit are for believers and their children, and those who by faith receive these blessings at the first Pentecost of the new covenant church are also baptized (Acts 2:1–41).
Many will participate in the new age of restoration as Gentiles and Jews together confess the name of the Lord and are joined together as the true Israel of God (cf. Ps. 87:4–6).

The Lord confronts the idols. On Isaiah’s polemic against idolatry (vv. 9–20), see note on 2:8.

**44:6 Redeemer.** See note on 35:9, 10.

**first ... last.** See note on 41:4.
God demonstrates His sovereignty over history through predictive prophecy. See 41:22, 26.

See note on 43:10.

**Rock.** See note on 8:14, 15; Deut. 32:4, 15, 31.

See note on 41:29.

**Their witnesses.** The “witnesses” could be the idols or their makers. Neither has any power of sight or understanding (Ps. 115:8).
The setting is a court of law (41:21).
An idol may be a work of art. But even the finest craftsman’s mortality is revealed in his hunger and thirst. How can a human make anything that is greater than himself (cf. 40:28)?
The carpenter makes his god in his own image (Deut. 4:16; Rom. 1:22, 23). Yet the true God has made us in His image (Gen. 1:27).

verse_quote: half of it he burns ... the rest he makes into a god.
note: The same substance is burned and venerated. How can the same thing be both firewood and a deity?, 17
They are utterly foolish (v. 9; 6:9, 10). The idol-worshiper becomes as blind and helpless as the idol that he worships.
The prophet employs ridicule to expose the foolishness of idolatry.
The conclusion: idolatry is a deception, a hoax. “A lie” is a common term in the prophets for an idol.
The Lord alone is redeemer (35:9, 10; 41:14 and notes).

All creation will praise God for His salvation of Israel. The natural order that furnishes materials such as wood and metal from which humans make idols is not as dumb and blind as human idol-worshipers are. Instead, it glorifies its creator.

**glorified.** God will glorify the redeemed, who in turn will lead many to praise the Lord for His mighty acts (4:2 note; 49:3; 55:5; 60:21; 61:3). Creation may rightly praise God, but the greatest praise that God receives is from those who have experienced His redemption.

The Lord’s care for His people started before they were born (Ps. 139:13). His redemption is therefore not based on our works, but solely on His electing grace (see Rom. 9:11). This is why He blots out our many transgressions and redeems us (v. 22).

False prophets.

**diviners.** Divination was strictly forbidden in Israel (2:6; 8:19 and notes).

These refer to the Lord’s revelations of His plan (11:2 note). He declares ahead of time His purposes through His servants, the prophets (Amos 3:7).

**servant.** See notes on 20:3; 41:8; 42:1.

**ruins.** The regions devastated by Babylon. The restoration of Judah is the beginning of a new stage in the history of redemption.

Possibly a reference to the crossing of the Red Sea (43:16, 19 and notes). The prophecy may have found a literal fulfillment when Cyrus diverted the water of the Euphrates River and marched his army through the water gates that allowed it to flow through the city of Babylon (45:2 note).

Kings were often called shepherds in the ancient Near East (2 Sam. 5:2; Jer. 3:15; cf. Mic. 5:4). The postexilic community is to know that Cyrus rules by God’s decree. Raising up a pagan ruler to fulfill the Lord’s purpose of bringing His people back to their homeland is as astonishing and miraculous an event as drying up rivers or providing water in the wilderness.

**Jerusalem ... temple.** These are rebuilt by Cyrus’s royal decree (Ezra 1:2–4; 6:3–5).

This title is not used elsewhere of anyone outside Israel, and its application to Cyrus would have shocked Isaiah’s original audience. It stresses the fact that the Lord can use anyone to accomplish His purposes, even pagan emperors. Identifying Judah’s deliverer by name many years ahead of time is a clear mark of the Lord’s sovereign power to predict and control the future.

**right hand I have grasped.** He rules by the Lord’s authority and has been commissioned by Him for a particular task (41:2; 48:14; cf. Pss. 2:8, 9; 110:1).

**nations ... kings.** See note on 41:2.

Bronze and iron are the hardest known materials at the time the prophecy is given; nothing can withstand the Lord’s Servant (cf. Ps. 107:16).

**doors.** The prophecy may have had a literal fulfillment when Cyrus used the gates that allowed the Euphrates to flow through Babylon (44:27 note).

Precious metals come from deep mines (Job 28:1–6). Cyrus plundered the fabulous wealth of Lydia in 546 B.C.

**call you by your name.** The Lord has raised up Cyrus and knows him (cf. 43:1 note).

See notes on 20:3; 41:8; 42:1. Cyrus’s success is not for his own sake but a means to God’s greater end, which is the deliverance of His people from exile.

**chosen.** See note on 14:1.

**name you.** As God’s “shepherd” (44:28) and “anointed” (v. 1), Cyrus has a title of honor.

**you do not know me.** Cyrus is an unbeliever.

verse_quote: from the rising of the sun and from the west.
note: The two opposites, the eastern and western horizon, encompass everyone in between.

See note on 27:11.

**light ... darkness.** The Lord asserts His power over two fundamental poles of reality, whose separation was the first step in the process of creating the world (Gen. 1:3, 4). The opposing terms “well-being” and “calamity” include the political realities that Cyrus will disturb in fulfilling the counsel of God.

Creation must prepare itself for the Lord’s act of redemption, described by two synonyms: “righteousness” and “salvation” (12:2; 26:17, 18 and notes). In Prov. 3:20, showers of rain are associated with creation, but whereas the earth sprouted green plants in the beginning, now it will sprout with salvation and righteousness.

verse_quote: Does the clay say to him who formed it.
note: The image of potter and clay is a common one for the Lord’s sovereignty over His people. He is their creator and, as such, He has the right to assign them their purpose and determine whether they are fulfilling it. Indeed, like a potter, the Lord literally formed the first man, Adam, from the dust of the ground (Gen. 2:7; cf. v. 12). Human beings have no rights independent of those assigned to them by the One who created them, and to seek such autonomy is to place oneself under a judgment curse (“woe”). Cf. Jer. 18:6; Rom. 9:20, 21.

Isaiah moves seamlessly from describing creation to describing history, for the same God is sovereign over both (cf. Is. 40). The same power that made the universe out of nothing is now exercised in redeeming His people from their bondage.

**not for price.** Although the Lord gives Cyrus a handsome reward (v. 3) for ransoming His people (43:3), this is not the reason Cyrus has liberated them.
See notes on 43:3; Ps. 68:31. Distant nations will come to worship the one God (Zech. 8:23; Eph. 3:6).

God is said to hide Himself when He seems not to be present to help His people (8:17; 54:8). He is also “hidden” in the sense that He is unaccountable to anyone, and His ways are often mysterious (55:8, 9; Ps. 77:19 note; Rom. 9:20; 11:33, 34).
God is unlike people and idols, who can never secure the future for themselves or for others (cf. Heb. 5:9).

This word is translated “without form” in Gen. 1:2. This was the beginning, not the end of creation. In the same way God does not invite people to seek Him to no purpose. He will carry through with what He has begun (55:11; 66:9) and answer those who seek Him (55:3; Matt. 11:28; Heb. 11:6). Just as He created the world to be peopled, so will His new heavens and new earth must be peopled with a redeemed humanity.

verse_quote: in secret, in a land of darkness.
note: The Lord’s revelation is unlike pagan oracles, which are obscure and ambiguous. The Lord’s revelation is clear and public, through the words of His prophets, though the outworking of His promises might not conform to human expectations (48:16). Nonetheless, it will be effective in bringing His chosen people into a true relationship with Him.
See v. 14 and note.

God’s promises are guaranteed by His own name, for there is no one greater by whom to swear (14:24; 62:8; cf. Gen. 22:16; Ex. 32:13; Heb. 6:13–18).

**a word that shall not return.** None of the Lord’s words shall be ineffective. See 55:11.

**every knee ... every tongue.** The goal of redemptive history is to bring Israel’s offspring to repentant submission before the Lord’s majesty (v. 14 and note; Rom. 14:11; 1 Cor. 15:25; Phil. 2:10, 11). Yet Israel’s offspring will include the ends of the earth as well, for God includes the Gentiles in His salvation (see v. 22).

Babylonian gods. Bel means “lord” and probably refers to Marduk, the most powerful god in the Babylonian pantheon, while Nebo (or Nabu) is the god of wisdom. In reality, neither has any true power or wisdom to offer.

The idols are dead weight, lifeless burdens on the animals that have to carry them, unlike the Lord who lifts His people up on eagle’s wings (see 40:31). The idols cannot even save themselves from going into captivity, let alone those who worship them. On Isaiah’s polemic against idolatry, see 2:8.

The small group that is saved out of the judgment. See note on 1:9.

**birth ... womb.** The Lord’s care is like that of a mother for her children—tender, attentive, and with the best interests of His people in mind (44:2 note; 49:5; cf. Deut. 1:31; Hos. 11:3, 4).

Unlike the powerless idols, the Lord is constant in His care for His people, from before their birth to their old age (Ps. 71:9, 18).

**I am he.** See note on 41:4.

verse_quote: To whom will you liken me.

note: A god that cannot move can do nothing to save or to judge.
See notes on 41:22; 42:9. This includes the Lord’s past acts of deliverance of His people and judgment on His enemies in which He demonstrated real power to direct the course of events.
Unlike Bel and Nebo (see v. 1), who have neither power nor wisdom, the Lord’s power establishes what His wisdom decrees. No power in earth or heaven can stand against His sovereign will.
Cyrus; see 41:2.

These are the transgressors of v. 8. As some in the first exodus looked back to Egypt (Num. 14:3), some in the second exodus remain in Babylon, doubting that the Lord could really bring about His promised salvation and restore the glory of His people—at least at any time in the near future (cf. Hag. 1:2).
See note on 1:8.

An oracle regarding the fall of Babylon, never to rise again. Her fall is the mirror image of Zion’s restoration, and it matches Jerusalem’s original fall (see 3:16–26).

**47:1–3** Babylon, the queen of nations, is commanded to descend from her throne and become a menial slave girl. In contrast, Zion, a captive slave girl, will be commanded to ascend her throne (52:1, 2). God has used the Babylonians to bring judgment on His own people, but they are proud and assume that their gods have given them victory.

**47:1 virgin daughter of Babylon.** The city of Babylon and its inhabitants. On the idiom, see note on 1:8.

**Chaldeans.** Babylonians. See note on 13:19.
All Babylon’s privileges and status will be removed. She will be humiliated.
See notes on 35:9; 41:14, as well as the promise in 43:14 to judge Babylon.
Her boast is based on her contempt for the truths that God rules history and that He will judge her for her cruelties (v. 6; Rev. 18:7). Her society and politics have no regard for the true God.
The Babylonians claim godlike power and self-existence for themselves, a glory that the Lord will not share with anyone (see 45:5, 6, 18, 21, 22; 46:9).

Babylon’s losses will occur suddenly.

**loss of children and widowhood.** Bereft of her husband and children, Babylon has no hope for the future and is consigned to slavery and extinction (cf. 49:21–23; 54:1–6).

**your many sorceries ... your enchantments.** The Babylonians are famous in Isaiah’s day for the study of magic, so much so that “Chaldean” comes to be a term for those who practice divination. Yet they place their trust in these things in vain.
Babylon’s traditions of religion, magic, and divination. See note on 44:25.
Their vaunted wisdom (see v. 10) will be of no value to them.
Isaiah mocks their confidence in divination.
Babylon depends on omens from the heavenly bodies for her decisions (Dan. 2:2).
See Rev. 18:17–19. Babylon’s astrologers practice their craft to save Bab­ylon from these prophecies (v. 13), but they cannot even save themselves (Dan. 2:10–13).

verse_quote: those ... who have done business with you.
note: Babylon’s trading partners, who will be unable to assist her when the day of judgment comes.

This final and urgent appeal is designed to lead deaf and blind Israel (vv. 6, 8; cf. 42:18–20; 46:3–12; 51:1) to recognize God’s ways in creation and in history (vv. 12, 16).

**but not in truth or right.** It is possible to be descended from Israel but not be part of the true Israel; the true Israel is known by sincere faith in the Lord (Rom. 2:28, 29; 9:6–8).
The Lord’s military title stresses His power to act, so His name is not merely a label but an expression of His character and power.
See notes on 41:22; 42:9.
Parts of the body associated with stubbornness (see Deut. 31:27; Ezek. 3:7).

verse_quote: from of old, before they came to pass.
note: The Lord alone decrees and executes His will according to His word. Yet His people are stubbornly attached to their idols, even after years of exile.

The evidence speaks for itself, if only they will believe God’s word. In the past the problem was that they were blind and deaf to the Lord’s message (see 6:10).

**new things, hidden things.** An era of salvation and kingdom righteousness begins with the restoration from exile, including God’s raising up Cyrus to set the Jews free (45:1), but these prophecies look forward ultimately to Christ’s coming and the growth of His kingdom in its fullness (45:15; Rev. 1:19).
See 1:2.

The exile has been a period of refining (1:22, 25; cf. Ezek. 22:18–22; 1 Pet. 1:7). Difficult though it was, their trial was not as severe as the refining of silver, which involves extremely high temperatures.

The Lord does everything for His own glory, which is good news for undeserving rebels. He will fulfill His original purpose for Abraham and his offspring in spite of their continual rebellion against Him.

Cf. Babylon’s boast in 47:8, 10. The Lord is truly the One who was there in the beginning and whose kingdom will never come to an end. The Creator of all things will accomplish His purpose for the universe, which is to have a sanctified, holy people that belong to Him and serve Him.
The Lord gives Cyrus his status and success.

verse_quote: from the beginning ... I have been there.
note: The Lord is the eternal God who speaks and acts (see vv. 12, 13). The last part of the verse refers to one of those acts, sending “me” (the Servant [see 49:1–3]) and His Spirit. Some see this verse as a reference to the Trinity. Christ is the servant who came into the world, sent by the Father and the Spirit. Salvation is the work of the triune God.

See notes on 35:9; 41:14.

**who teaches you to profit.** Unlike the idols, whose service is without profit (44:9), serving the Lord is not a wasted endeavor.

verse_quote: Oh that you had paid attention.
note:
God reveals a compassionate longing for His people to find their peace in living for Him. Because they have rebelled against the Lord, they have experienced great and needless pain and loss throughout their history (see 1:5, 6).

**river ... waves of the sea.** These similes represent abundant life (66:12; Amos 5:24).

**righteousness.** See note on 1:21. Peace and righteousness go together (v. 22; 26:3 note; 32:17; 54:13, 14; 60:17; Ps. 85:10; Heb. 7:2).
The promise first made to Abraham (Gen. 12:2; 22:17).
The prophet remembers the exodus from Egypt and how God provided for His people then (41:17–20; 43:19–21; 44:3; cf. Ex. 17:6; Ps. 105:41).

See note on v. 18. This is true both for the nations and for those who claim to be the Lord’s people but are simply going through the motions (48:1, 2). Rest can be found nowhere other than in the Lord.

The second of the four “Servant Songs” (42:1–9; 49:1–7; 50:4–11; 52:13–53:12).

**49:1 called ... name.** The faithful Servant is called “Israel” (v. 3; 43:1; 44:2, 24; 45:3 and notes). He is distinct from unfaithful Israel, and He Himself has a mission to the tribes of Jacob as well as the task of accomplishing Israel’s unfulfilled mission to the Gentiles (vv. 5, 6; 42:18; 46:12; 48:1 and notes).

The Servant conquers through preaching (11:4 note; 51:16 note; 61:1). God’s words are effective (40:8; 45:19; 55:10, 11).

**sharp sword ... polished arrow.** These metaphors portray the effectiveness of the word, which in the NT context is explicitly the word of Christ (Eph. 6:17; Heb. 4:12; Rev. 1:16; 2:12, 16; 19:15).
See notes on 20:3; 41:8; 42:1.

The Servant’s complaint is fulfilled in Christ’s rejection and suffering (42:2 note).

**right.** See 40:10; cf. Gen. 15:1. The Servant triumphs through weakness and is vindicated (50:8) and rewarded after His death and resurrection (53:8–10).

See note on 27:11.

**bring ... gathered.** One purpose of the Servant is to reconcile the Jews to God.

A second purpose of the Servant is to bring the gospel to the nations (Luke 2:32; Acts 13:47; 26:23). He fulfills the call of Abraham (Gen. 12:3; 22:18) and of Israel (Ex. 19:5, 6). Today the ascended Christ brings the gospel to the nations through His body, the church (Matt. 28:18–20; 1 Pet. 2:9, 10).

**to the end of the earth.** See Acts 1:8.

See note on 41:14.

**servant of rulers.** Paradoxically, the King who humbles himself to become a servant of rulers will Himself receive their homage (4:2; 45:24; 52:15). God will exalt the despised and rejected Servant.

This time stands in contrast to the day of vengeance (12:2; 34:8 and notes; cf. 35:4; 59:17, 18; 61:2; 63:4; 2 Cor. 6:2).

**a covenant to the people.** See note on 42:7. The God who covenanted to give Abraham the land will fulfill His promise through His Servant.

**establish ... apportion.** This restoration begins with the return from exile (44:26; 45:8 note).

Those still in exile. See notes on 42:7; 51:14; 61:1.

**darkness.** See notes on 5:30 and 9:2.

**feed ... pasture.** The Servant is Israel’s shepherd and king (40:11).
Isaiah alludes to the exodus from Egypt (42:16; 48:21; Ex. 15:13).
See notes on 11:16 and 40:4.

The salvation of true Israel is in view here (11:11 note).

**Syene.** Hb. _sinim_, which the Dead Sea Scrolls relate to Syene, which is Aswan, in southern Egypt (cf. Ezek. 29:10; 30:6).
See note on 14:7. Creation, which has witnessed the Lord’s acts of judgment, will now burst into praise, so great is the Lord’s salvation of His people.

God seemed to have abandoned Judah during the exile (40:27; 54:7). Yet it is even more impossible for God to forget those with whom He had entered a covenant than for a mother to forget her own child. “Remembering” here includes not merely calling someone to mind but appropriately acting on that thought.

Though the Lord’s memory is infallible, He had written a permanent reminder on His hands to constantly remind Him of His people.

**walls.** See note on 26:1. City walls form the core of the city’s defenses, so if the Lord remembers the walls of the city, she cannot fall. Rebuilding the walls of Jerusalem is a crucial step to removing Judah’s shame after the exile (see Neh. 1).
Zion’s children (see v. 20).

The prophecy of vv. 19–21 looks beyond the return at the time of Cyrus. Nehemiah later builds only a small city, but the promised blessing bursts the boundaries of such historical realities. The prophecy is fulfilled in the new Israel, the church (54:1–3; Zech. 2:4, 5).

Judah’s perspective has been too narrow. She has seen herself as widowed and alone, abandoned by the Lord, her true husband. Yet she has not been abandoned and forgotten. On the contrary, while she has been weeping, the Lord has been preparing a lasting legacy for her, preserving the remnant that He will bring safely back from Babylon.
Not just Babylon, as is the case at the time of Cyrus (v. 19 note; cf. Rom. 11:26).

Nations that formerly have oppressed Israel will come to serve her and care for her. Ultimately, the promise is fulfilled as the nations come to serve Christ and His church, the true Israel, and find salvation in so doing (Gen. 12:3).

**lick the dust.** On the “Black Obelisk” of Shalman­eser III, Jehu, king of Israel, is shown bowing to the ground before the Assyrian ruler.

**wait.** See 40:31 and note. Just as faith is a key theme in the opening chapters of Isaiah’s prophecy, waiting is crucial in the later chapters. In the face of a difficult present and a dark immediate future, God’s people need to look to the ultimate end of all things in order to live faithfully in the present.

The Lord takes up the case of the needy and is just in His retribution (v. 26; Rev. 16:6; 18:20). What is impossible for people, rescuing prey from the mighty, is easy for the Lord to accomplish (see Matt. 19:26).

See 9:20.

**know.** See note on 52:6.

**Mighty One.** Isaiah reveals the vindication of the people of God. God Himself will fight for His people and redeem them from all adversity.

The inhabitants of Jerusalem who were taken into the Babylonian exile are figuratively described as God’s wife.

**certificate of divorce.** Had the Lord issued such a divorce, He could not have taken Israel back (Deut. 24:1–4; Jer. 3:1, 8). Instead, even though He sent her away for her transgressions, He has not permanently dissolved the relationship.

**creditors.** Had the Lord sold Israel to creditors, He would have lost authority over their destiny (cf. 2 Kin. 4:1; Neh. 5:5).

**for your iniquities.** Since Israel was sold in payment for the debt of her sins, the Redeemer has the responsibility to buy them back (41:14; 52:3).

verse_quote: Why ... was there no one to answer?
note:
Israel should be hoping and praying for redemption in light of the Lord’s past faithfulness. Though it seems that everyone has given up hope of salvation (see 49:14), there is no diminution in the Lord’s ability or desire to rescue His people from their sins.

**I dry up the sea.** As at the time of the exodus from Egypt.

The third of four “Servant Songs” (42:1–9; 49:1–7; 50:4–11; 52:13–53:12). The reproach against believing Israel in the exile (51:7) anticipates the rejection of Jesus Christ.

**50:4 word.** See notes on 45:23; 49:2.

**weary.** By His words, the Servant does what God has promised to do. See Is. 40:29–31; Jer. 31:25.

**he awakens my ear.** Unlike Israel’s deafness toward the Lord (6:10), the Servant is constantly listening to God’s direction.
Unlike Israel in 1:2, the Servant is obedient to the Lord.

Jesus Christ suffered such injustice as part of His obedience to God (53:5, 11, 12; Matt. 27:26; John 19:1). One would expect the Servant’s constant obedience to result in blessing. Instead, though the Servant is free from Israel’s rebelliousness, He will still experience a judgment similar to the one that the nation bore for her sin (see 1:5, 6).

**pull out the beard.** An act of humiliation (2 Sam. 10:4, 5; Neh. 13:25).

Resolved and determined to continue in obedience to the Lord in the face of opposition (cf. Ezek. 3:8, 9; Jer. 1:18; Luke 9:51).

**not be put to shame.** The Servant will not be put to shame by defeat, but He will ultimately be vindicated by the Lord. None of His adversaries can withstand the Lord’s help.

verse_quote: fears the LORD ... obeys the voice of his servant.
note:
These amount to the same thing. The Servant’s words are God’s words.

**him who walks in darkness.** See 9:2. Those living in difficult circumstances who cannot see where their paths are heading need to trust in the Lord and rely on His faithfulness.

The opposite of trusting the Lord in the darkness Refers to human attempts to discern the future. They undertake plans relying on their own strength and wisdom, rather than on God’s revelation, and bring themselves to ruin as a result. The fire that they have kindled to bring them light will itself be the source of their torment.

The same group referred to in 50:10 as those who fear the Lord.

**rock ... quarry.** They are asked to remember their descent from Abraham and Sarah (Deut. 26:5; cf. Ezek. 16:6). Their origin was modest, and they came from an area not far away from where the exiles are living in Babylon. Yet God called them, brought them to the Land of Promise, and built them into a great nation so that they could be a light to the surrounding nations as they trusted in Him (see Gen. 12:1–3).

For this “garden of the Lord,” see Gen. 2:8; Ezek. 28:13; 31:8, 9. The promise here is a transformation from curse to blessing.

**joy and gladness.** In Zion, joy will replace sorrow (v. 11). In effect, the people will regain the lost paradise of God (9:3; 12:3 and notes).This, of course, necessitates that the Lord deal with the sin that drove them out of the garden.
As the source of the law in the last days, the Servant establishes justice and thereby, fulfills the role that the temple played in the earlier prophecy (2:2–4; 42:1–4, 6; 49:6).

The day of the Lord that brings judgment and redemption is always imminent, though scoffers doubt that God will act (46:13; Zeph. 1:14; 1 Thess. 5:4–11; James 5:8; 2 Pet. 3:1–7). They think, wrongly, that the Lord is as powerless as the idols.

The present creation is destined to be replaced, but the Lord’s salvation lasts forever (50:9; cf. Pss. 68:2; 102:3, 26; Hos. 13:3; see also Is. 24:4; 34:4; Heb. 1:10–12; 2 Pet. 3:10). As a result, storing up treasure in the things of this world is a foolish strategy (Matt. 6:19–21).

verse_quote: in whose heart is my law.
note: Notice the spiritual reality of the covenant (Jer. 31:31–34; Ezek. 36:27) in contrast to the state of the people in 29:13 and 48:1.

verse_quote: the moth will eat them up.
note: Like earthly treasure, earthly opposition is transitory and powerless to do lasting harm; the Lord alone has power over our eternal destiny (Matt. 10:28).

The command implies that the Lord has appeared to be asleep (40:27, 28; Ps. 44:23).

**Rahab.** See note on 30:7. The spiritual enemies of God’s salvation are portrayed as the forces of chaos and evil, familiar figures in ancient Near Eastern mythology. Such forces are overcome by God, not Israel or any other human power. In ch. 30, Rahab represents Egypt; here, likewise, Israel’s deliverance from Egypt at the time of the exodus is in the prophet’s mind.

verse_quote: Was it not you who dried up the sea.
note: Cf. Ps. 89:9 and Job 26:12.

Redemption is never simply deliverance from pain. It always has as its goal the people of God gathered in His presence to worship. New acts of salvation furnish the material for new songs of joyful praise.

This is emphatic as in v. 15. The double pronoun corresponds to the double command, “Awake, awake” (v. 9).

**grass.** See 37:27; 40:7, 8; Ps. 129:6 and notes. The temporary nature of humanity is always contrasted with the Lord’s eternal nature, which ensures His ability to accomplish all of His plans. This news should comfort the Lord’s people as they experience oppression and suffering: those who presently rule over them do not control their destiny.
Sheol, often simply “the grave” in the OT, but Isaiah frequently uses it for the shadowy home of the unrighteous dead. See note on 5:14.

verse_quote: stirs up the sea so that its waves roar.
note: See notes on 51:9, 10. This power over the sea is representative of His power over all creation (Job 26:12; Ps. 107:25; Jer. 31:35).

The remnant of faithful Israelites have received new words of gladness and joy from the Lord, to replace the old words of sadness and sorrow (see v. 11). They exist under His providential care and protection.

Double imperatives are also found in vv. 1, 9; 52:1, 11 (cf. Eph. 5:14). See note on v. 9. This is Jerusalem’s appropriate response to the Lord’s rousing Himself to action on their behalf.

**cup of his wrath.** An image of God’s judgment (63:6; Ps. 75:8; Jer. 25:15–31; Ezek. 23:31–34; John 18:11; Rev. 14:10; 16:19).

verse_quote: none to take her by the hand.
note: Children may sometimes be able to assist drunk parents to get home safely, but there has been no such help available for Jerusalem, for her children have also drunk from the cup of the Lord’s wrath.
The graceful animal depicts Jerusalem, surrounded by the enemy and in danger of dying.
Jerusalem’s staggering is not caused by intoxication but by the Lord’s wrath, which has now run its course (40:2 note). It is now her enemies’ turn to feel the weight of God’s judgment.
Preeminently the Babylonians (Lam. 1:4, 5). The ones who have mistreated the Judeans will themselves experience God’s wrath.

Now the same imperative that was addressed to the Lord in 51:9 is addressed to His people: they are to rouse themselves to praise in response to the Lord’s new acts of deliverance. Zion is called to wake up and recognize that the long night of exile is over at last.

**beautiful garments.** Where earlier she was stripped naked for her adultery, now Jerusalem is magnificently dressed as a royal wife (61:10; Rev. 3:4, 5, 18; 4:4; cf. 47:1–3). The Lord has removed her defiled clothing, providing her with fresh garments of holiness that she should now wear (cf. Zech. 3:1–6). In Eph. 4:22–24, Paul uses the metaphor of putting off and putting on clothing, while in Eph. 6 he unpacks what that new clothing looks like, including a reference to Is. 52:7: feet shod with the gospel of peace.

**the uncircumcised and the unclean.** The wicked will have no share in the city of God (48:22; Nah. 1:15; Rev. 21:27; 22:14, 15). These have been both a temptation and a torment to the Lord’s people, but both problems will be removed.
Jerusalem and its citizens were under the yoke of the Bab­ylonians, but now that yoke has been broken off, they should live as free servants of God (see Rom. 6:11–14).

The idols have given Israel nothing. Since no payment was made, the transaction was not finalized.

**without money.** Salvation is free (45:13; 55:1). Yet God still demands a perfect payment for our redemption, as becomes clear in the following passages.

Israel was dependent on Egypt’s promised hospitality, but Egypt betrayed that trust.

**the Assyrian.** The three great oppressions of the Lord’s old covenant people are bondage in Egypt in the time of Moses (the past), the exile of the northern kingdom of Israel by the Assyrians in 722 B.C. (the present in Isaiah’s own time), and the subjugation by the Babylonians in 586 B.C. (still future from Isaiah’s perspective).

Israel’s sin and consequent judgment have defiled the Lord’s name by bringing into question His ability to fulfill His plans (see Ezek. 20). Therefore, the Lord has acted to deliver His people not for their sake alone, but for the sake of His own reputation.
