Alludes to Ex. 3:13, 14; 6:2. The Lord glorifies His name through inspiring Isaiah’s prophecies and bringing them to pass, demonstrating His power to fulfill His purposes in history.

The focus is still on Judah’s response, instead of the deliverance itself. Rather than depicting the battle, the image is of messengers running from the scene of battle across the hills to Zion with the good news that God reigns. They prefigure the evangelists who will announce the gospel of Jesus Christ (Rom. 10:15; Eph. 6:15). The Lord’s victory ushers in redemption and peace for His people because their God (rather than the idols) has been shown to reign.

Or perhaps “shouting for joy.” The result of God’s deliverance of His people is that they join their voices together in praising Him (see 14:7; 35:2; 44:23; 51:11).

**waste places of Jerusalem.** See 51:3. Restoration, after the Babylonian exile of the sixth century B.C., begins with the rebuilding of Jerusalem’s ruins (Ezra 3:8–13; Neh. 6:15–7:3). In the same sense, Christ is rebuilding His people who were being destroyed by sin, creating something profitable and fruitful out of what was once a barren desert (1 Pet. 2:5).

These people represent all of Zion and serve God as priests. They must be consecrated for holy service and remain undefiled (2 Cor. 6:17; Heb. 12:14; 1 Pet. 2:1–12; Rev. 18:4). The return of the sacred vessels from exile in Babylon is highly symbolic of the restoration of the people (see 2 Kin. 25:13–17; Ezra 1:1–11).

The contrast is with the exodus from Egypt. Ex. 12:11 and Deut. 16:3 are the only other passages where this phrase occurs.

**before you ... rear guard.** An allusion to the pillar of cloud and fire that protected Israel in their flight from Egypt (42:16; 58:8; cf. Ex. 13:21, 22; 14:19, 20). The same protection will be extended to His people in their new exodus from Babylon (see note on 40:1–55:13). God’s presence guides His people into the fullness and brilliance of His everlasting kingdom (4:5, 6; 49:10).

The last of the four “Servant Songs” (42:1–9; 49:1–7; 50:4–11; 52:13–53:12). The Lord’s triumphant victory is revealed through crushing oppression and judgment. How does the Lord provide those glorious robes of righteousness for His defiled bride? How does the strong arm of the Lord win His victory? He accomplishes it by afflicting His obedient Servant in our place. This “Suffering Servant” is Jesus Christ. This passage is quoted or referred to many times in the NT. Christ’s suffering in the place of His sheep gives them eternal life. This song contains five chiastic stanzas of three verses each: 52:13–15; 53:1–3, 4–6, 7–9, 10–12. Stanzas 1 and 5 focus on the victory of the Servant, stanzas 2 and 4 focus on the realities of His suffering, and the central stanza shows us the reason for His suffering.

**52:13–15** The Lord vindicates and glorifies His servant. The song begins at the end, with the triumphant outcome of the Servant’s suffering. Otherwise, one might fail to see that His suffering is indeed triumphant.

**52:13 act wisely.** The Servant will discern and perform God’s will, achieving His glorious purpose as a result (Luke 24:26; 1 Pet. 5:10).
The poem cuts from the exultation of final victory to the agony of apparent defeat. Christ was disfigured by the abuse He suffered from Roman soldiers.

Participation in the benefits of a sacrifice is indicated by receiving the sprinkling of blood by the Servant, who here takes up a priestly role. See Ex. 24:8 and note; Lev. 4:1–5:13 note; and Heb. 9:19 note. Israel is not the only beneficiary of the cleansing; the nations are sprinkled as well. Here there is a reversal of Is. 6, where those who hear do not understand and those who have eyes do not see.

verse_quote: Who has believed what he has heard from us.
note: Will God’s own people receive the gospel proclaimed by the believing remnant? Initially at least, the answer is no. Many nations hear and understand but “we” (the Jewish nation) do not esteem Him (v. 3).

His origins are not promising (Zech. 4:10; John 1:46). He comes without pomp or honor, like a root in the parched soil—though He is the promised root from the stump of Jesse (cf. 11:1).

**no form or majesty.** Unlike Saul, or even David (1 Sam. 9:2; 16:12).

See 49:7. Cf. Ps. 22:6; Lam. 1:1–3; 2:15, 16.

**a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief.** The word for “grief” here is more often translated “sickness.” Human beings flee from suffering and weakness, yet the Servant deliberately embraces both.

The central stanza of the poem draws attention to the reason for this suffering of the Servant. It is vicarious suffering in our place—that is, on behalf of His wandering people. The prophet includes himself in this redemptive experience, just as he included himself in the condemnation for sin in ch. 6.

**smitten by God.** They believe this about the Servant because the law said, “a hanged man is cursed by God” (Deut. 21:23; cf. Gal. 3:13). The onlookers thought Christ was suffering only what He deserved, but His experience of pain and anguish was for His people (1 Pet. 2:24). He did not merely suffer physical pain and human abandonment; on the cross, He was even abandoned by God, receiving the hellish fate that all people deserve. The extremity of Jesus’ suffering shows that His compassion is real and not theoretical (Heb. 2:17, 18).
The sufferings of Christ remove the penalty that His people otherwise owe, and as a result He will undo the effects of sin in them. Death itself will be undone at last (1 Cor. 15:26).

Even as we sinned, so He died for us (2 Cor. 5:14, 15). See theological note “Definite Atonement” on p. 1875.

**sheep ... astray.** See 1 Pet. 2:25.

**laid.** The guilt of our sins was transferred to Jesus, and He offered Himself as a sacrifice in our place. As Paul wrote, God “made him to be sin who knew no sin” (2 Cor. 5:21).
Christ is the Lamb of God (John 1:29; 1 Cor. 5:7; Rev. 5:6) in obedience and submission to God (cf. Matt. 26:63; 27:12, 14; 1 Pet. 2:23). We went astray like sheep and He paid the penalty.
He is put to death as a result of injustice.

He is deprived of justice and descendants, and buried with the unrighteous rich who were the subject of so much prophetic rebuke in the earlier chapters of Isaiah. The Servant’s suffering for sinners has thus been successfully completed. Ironically, this prophecy is fulfilled through the intervention of the righteous Joseph of Arimathea, who gave Jesus a tomb in which to be buried.

**violence ... deceit.** He is wise and righteous (1 Pet. 2:22), but died a criminal’s death (Luke 23:33). He doesn’t open His mouth in deceit any more than He has in self-defense (v. 7).

verse_quote: it was the will of the Lord.
note:
This amazing statement is true because Christ was delivered up “according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God” (Acts 2:23).

**offspring.** Those who come to life through His death (John 12:24; Gal. 3:29).

**prosper in his hand.** Only through the Lord’s will to crush His Servant can the Lord’s will prosper in His hand and give Him many spiritual offspring as the fruit of this prosperity.

Refers to His insight into the divine plan (52:13 note). Jesus didn’t wrestle sinners to safety out of the hands of an angry God. His sacrifice to save sinners was in perfect harmony with the will of the Father.

**righteous.** See Rom. 5:19.

**accounted righteous.** Christ’s righteousness is imputed to His people (53:6 note), and in return He accepted their guilt so as to “bear their iniquities.” This is a declarative change in status that comes to sinners from outside themselves, not a transformative change within them. See theological note “Justification by Faith” on p. 2078.

The Lord divides the spoils of victory with His triumphant Servant (52:13).

**poured out his soul.** He gives Himself for the sins of others (v. 4; Luke 22:37; Phil. 2:7, 8; Heb. 9:28; 1 Pet. 2:24).

**intercession.** He prays for sinners (Luke 23:34; Heb. 7:25).

See note on 14:7.

**barren ... desolate.** In exile, Judah and Israel felt forsaken by God and did not experience His blessing. Barrenness was a great reproach to a woman in the ancient world, and was often seen as a curse. Yet barrenness also had a positive history as God’s preparation for spiritual fruitfulness, as in the case of Abraham and Sarah (see 51:2).

**more than the children.** The NT applies this verse to “the Jerusalem above ... our mother” (Gal. 4:26, 27; cf. Heb. 12:22). See 49:21; 53:10.

The tent is enlarged in anticipation of a great increase in the number of occupants (cf. 26:15; 33:20; 49:19 note; Zech. 2:1–5; cf. Jer. 10:20). This allusion has to do with the prophetic oracle of Noah at Gen. 9:25–27, which in turn parallels the first announcement of the gospel in Gen. 3:15–21 and the promises made to Abram in Gen. 12:1, 2.

The expansion will be so great that they will possess the cities of their enemies (11:14 note; Gen. 22:17; 28:14). Yet as the previous chapters have made clear, that occupation will be a blessing to those from many nations who turn to the Lord through the Servant’s ministry.

Israel’s infidelity led to its oppression by Egypt and Assyria (52:4; Jer. 31:19). See note on 52:4.

**reproach of your widowhood.** This image represents the Babylonian exile (vv. 6–8).

Far from being a widow, Israel’s husband is her creator. The Lord has not rescued His people in order to keep them at a distance but for a close and intimate relationship with Him.

**the Holy One of Israel is your Redeemer.** See notes on 41:14. The title “Redeemer” recurs in v. 8.

**God of the whole earth.** The titles in v. 5 show that God did not give up Zion out of weakness or necessity (50:1–3). Now that He has brought her back to Him, no one can snatch her out of His hand.
See note on 49:14. Israel’s sin drove the Lord away (see Ezek. 8–11). Yet even Israel’s sin cannot thwart the Lord’s plan for her redemption.
The Lord’s anger is temporary but His mercy and forgiveness are everlasting (Ps. 30:5).

At the time of the flood, the Lord made a covenant with creation, symbolized by the rainbow, that He would never again send such a destructive flood (Gen. 9:1–17). Here He makes a commitment to never again bring such destructive anger to bear upon His people.

In our experience the mountains and hills seem permanent and unchanging, but the commitment of God to His people will remain when they are gone (51:6; Ps. 46:2, 3; Matt. 24:35; Heb. 1:10–12).

**my covenant of peace.** Cf. Ezek. 34:25–31. This covenant of peace is impossible without the making of a new covenant, for the old covenant brought only destruction to the people because of their sin (Jer. 31:31–34).

Represents the day of the Lord’s wrath.

**lay ... sapphires.** Describe the beauty and glory of Zion, the city of God, as if she were built out of precious stones (Rev. 21:19). It is difficult to identify exactly which gemstones are being referred to in the Hebrew.

verse_quote: all your children shall be taught by the
note: LORD**.** In the past, the next generation tended to forget God’s great acts of deliverance. But in future, the Lord Himself will take up their lessons, ensuring that they remember the stories clearly (see Jer. 31:34).
In the past, the nations that came against Israel (Assyria and Babylon) did so at the Lord’s direction. Now, however, anyone who assaults Israel will have the Lord to reckon with.
Since God is the creator of all, He is sovereign over what people are able to achieve. As a result, no one can successfully formulate a plan against God’s people without His permission.

The covenant and its promises, especially the promise of God’s protection and righteousness (1:21 note). This does not rule out trials and tribulation while God’s people are in the world. Jesus promises His followers no less (John 16:33). Yet He also reminds them in the same context that He has overcome the world.

This address follows logically on the previous section and expresses the worldwide applicability of the gospel.

**thirsts ... no money.** The thirst is for spiritual things that money cannot buy (52:3; Deut. 8:3; Pss. 42:2; 63:1; Prov. 9:5, 6; Matt. 5:6; John 7:37, 38; Rev. 21:6; 22:17).

**waters.** Isaiah frequently describes the new era of salvation, God’s kingdom and its divine blessings, in terms of an abundance of water (1:30, 31 note).

**buy ... without money.** This paradox signifies that salvation is a free gift for anyone who desires it (Matt. 11:28; Rom. 10:13; Titus 3:5). The primary qualification for receiving the gospel is to know that you are needy, and that you don’t have the resources to save yourself.

**wine and milk.** Symbols of complete satisfaction. God’s gift of salvation is even better than water for the thirsty or bread for the hungry; it is the richest of fare (see v. 2). Jesus’ first miracle, turning water into wine at Cana of Galilee (John 2:1–11), points to this truth.

verse_quote: Why do you spend your money.
note:
Unbelief is costly and ultimately unsatisfying.

**eat what is good.** See 1:19.

The promises of the Davidic covenant are now extended to all who come to God.

**everlasting covenant.** See 61:8; Jer. 32:40; Ezek. 37:26. Because God’s people have broken the Sinai covenant continually, a new covenant is needed that will bring lasting blessing to the people. In the covenant as given to David, God promised him a permanent throne and lasting dynasty (2 Sam. 7:12–16; 1 Kin. 8:23–26; Ps. 89:27–37). He pledged that David’s royal house would rule over the nations. Yet David and his offspring also sinned against God and broke the covenant (see Jer. 22:30). A new Israel and a new David are needed to uphold the covenant forever. These elements are fulfilled in Christ and His church (4:2; 7:14; 9:6; 11:1, 2 and notes).
This was accomplished especially by raising Jesus Christ, of the house of David, from the dead (Acts 13:34).
Whereas “you” is plural in v. 3, here it is singular, referring to the Servant. The Servant will draw the nations to find blessing in Him through His vicarious suffering (see 52:15).

verse_quote: Seek the LORD while he may be found.
note: The offer of salvation is not permanently open; it is necessary to respond to God’s gracious invitation while one may do so.

God requires living faith, which is demonstrated in repentance and change of behavior (James 2:18; 1 John 1:3–5).

**compassion ... abundantly pardon.** The prophet repeats the invitation of 1:18 with great boldness and directness.

verse_quote: my thoughts are not your thoughts.
note: Specifically, God’s thoughts concerning grace exceed human imagination (64:4; 1 Cor. 2:9; Eph. 3:20; Rom. 11:33). Yet this is also true of His providence, which often leads down unexpected pathways. It is to be expected that the sheep will not always understand their Shepherd’s leading.

The rain falls abundantly and of its own accord, and in a familiar but mysterious way produces plants and useful crops, evidently for the purpose of supplying people’s needs. The divine purpose in this is applied figuratively to the word of God in order to distinguish it from fallible human thoughts and plans. It also speaks of the Lord’s word as His decree by which He governs history. It never returns without accomplishing God’s sovereign purposes. Cf. 40:8., 11

The exodus from Babylon, like the exodus from Egypt, is a picture of how God delivers His people from their sins (48:20, 21; 52:11, 12; John 10:3; Col. 1:13).

**singing ... clap.** Creation rejoices in God’s acts of redemption (44:23; 49:13; Ps. 96:11–13).

Thorns and briers were earlier signs of God’s judgment (e.g. 7:23). By contrast, the cypress is an impressive tree where majestic birds rest. Judgment is now replaced by salvation (5:6; 32:13; 41:19).

**everlasting sign.** Cf. the rainbow in Gen. 9:8–17.

These prophecies are addressed to the exiles returned from Babylon before the rebuilding of the temple in 520 B.C. (64:8–12). They still suffer from idolatry, hypocrisy, and indifference. Isaiah prophesies concerning their responsibilities toward the coming glorious kingdom and the certainty of its arrival.

**56:1 will come.** See 50:8; 51:5; Phil. 4:5. Since the Lord’s deliverance of His people is imminent, His people should lead lives in keeping with that reality.

Keeping this day holy (Ex. 31:13–17) signifies loyalty to the Lord and to His covenant (58:13; Ezek. 20:20). Failure to observe the Sabbath was one of the sins that resulted in the exile (2 Chr. 36:21).

Eunuchs were normally excluded from the covenant community, along with (unconverted) foreigners (Deut. 23:1). The Ethiopian eunuch of Acts 8:26–39 fulfills this promise through faith in Jesus, the Servant of Isa. 53. As Philip reads the scroll of Isaiah with the Ethiopian eunuch, he doubtless draws the man’s attention to this passage, since his companion is both a foreigner and a eunuch.

**a dry tree.** Not able to bear fruit. The Lord will give them a lasting legacy in spite of their physical impairment, just as barren Jerusalem will bear children (54:1).

Those with disabilities could not enter the temple in Jerusalem, as a sign of the spiritual wholeness that the Lord requires of His worshipers. That eunuchs (vv. 3, 4) will have an everlasting name in God’s house is a sign of the comprehensive spiritual restoration that is coming. The restoration will bring into the everlasting temple those who could not be brought in under the old covenant.

**everlasting name.** Everlasting life in God’s temple (v. 7; 2:2; Ps. 23:6; Acts 8:27, 36–38).

The verb here is formed from the same root as the name “Levi.” Foreigners who become part of God’s people will have the same privileges of service that the Levites alone previously enjoyed. The Lord’s true servants are evidenced by their faith rather than by simple heredity.

Being here means being included in the covenant and enjoying the life of communion with God. Prayer was a central part of the ministry of the temple, for the people experienced the presence of the Lord there. (2:2–4; Ps. 15:1; cf. 1 Kin. 8:41–43; Mark 11:17).

The Lord gathers Jews and non-Jews into one community (John 10:16). If the Lord can save foreigners who trust in Him, how much more is He able to save the remnant of His Israel when they trust in Him?
Hostile nations (18:6; Ezek. 34:5, 8, 25).

They warn the city of approaching danger. The prophets were called to be spiritual watchmen (21:6; Jer. 6:17; Ezek. 3:17; 33:2–7).

**blind.** Blindness is a spiritual condition here. See note on 29:18.

**dogs.** In Isaiah’s day, dogs are considered unclean, undesirable scavengers. The only value of such animals is the possibility that they might bark at strangers. Yet here, instead of barking a warning, they love to sleep and dream. They are representative of leaders who serve themselves instead of the people.
Rulers (v. 10 note; Ezek. 34:1–6; cf. 40:11 note). Rather than following the Lord’s guidance, these shepherds have turned to their own way, like sheep (see 53:6).
See 22:13 and note; Luke 12:19; James 4:13.

The shepherds ought to protect the righteous, but instead they allow the righteous to suffer injustice and persecution. Paradoxically, the death of the righteous means that they enter into His peace, while those left behind are the ones who truly suffer.
See note on 2:6; Deut. 18:10. The “sons of sorceresses” are those who share the sorceress’s characteristics and devotion to the occult.
The ungodly are filled with sarcasm and criticism (cf. 5:18, 19; 28:9, 10; 37:3).

Sacred groves of trees are often the locations of pagan places of worship (Deut. 12:2).

**children.** Child sacrifice is part of the worship of the Ammonite god Molech (v. 9 note; cf. 2 Kin. 23:10; Ps. 106:37, 38; Jer. 7:31; Ezek. 20:28, 31).

**valleys ... clefts.** Secret, hidden places (2:21; 7:19 note). The implication is that their practices are shameful.
Presumably these are used in pagan rituals, but the details are obscure.
The people have been involved in immoral and idolatrous practices at the hilltop shrines (Hos. 4:13). Their relation with these false gods is compared to sexual union., 8

The name of their god, “Molech,” is similar to the Hb. word for “king” and is probably what is meant here. Alternatively, it may refer to the pursuit of political alliances, which the prophet sees as a form of idolatry.

**sent down.** Isaiah describes the energy they have spent in willing service of their idols.

**Sheol.** This charge of visiting the realm of the dead (5:14 note) is either a figure of speech to express the depths to which they have sunk, or a reference to necromancy (communicating with the dead).
They have found a deceptive liveliness in immorality and idolatry that led to death. They have been passionately committed to their pagan forms of worship.

verse_quote: Have I not held my peace.
note: Because the Lord has not intervened to bring their evil to an end, they assume that His inactivity means acceptance. As a result, they fear the surrounding nations far more than they fear the Lord.
This is sarcasm; the threat is to declare their sins (cf. 58:2, 3; 64:6).
This promise is the blessing Jesus proclaimed to the meek (v. 15; Matt. 5:5). There is still a remnant whose trust is in the Lord.

See notes on 11:16; 40:3.

**obstruction.** This includes, but is not limited to, the idolatry and immorality described in vv. 3–13. Nothing can stand in the way of the Lord redeeming His people.

**my people’s way.** See note on 40:1.

An epithet for the Lord (6:1).

**high and holy place.** The Lord is transcendent over creation, yet He is nonetheless not far from those who call on His name.

**contrite and lowly spirit.** Those who submit to God’s law and repent under His judgment (Pss. 34:17, 18; 51:17; 1 Pet. 5:6).

In God’s grace, judgment will end and God will create salvation (54:9; 57:18, 19; Ps. 130:3, 4). The human spirit and mortal flesh cannot endure forever in such a conflict. The Lord knows exactly how much judgment is necessary to restore the backslider.

The Lord is physician (30:26 note), guide (49:10 note), and evangelist (40:1 note).

**mourners.** Those who lament Jerusalem’s destruction (64:10–12; 25:8 note).

Praise (Heb. 13:15).

**Peace, peace.** Unlike the false prophets, when the Lord declares peace, He accomplishes it for His people.
The wicked are constantly in motion, restless, and causing problems (Jude 13). There is no peace to be found among such people.
Unlike the silent dogs of 56:10, Isaiah is called to declare God’s word faithfully, exposing the people’s sins so that they may be convicted and repent (see 57:15).

The people are very religious, but they are not righteous. They have the outward form of religion but not its power (2 Tim. 3:5). This is revealed by their anger when God refuses to bless their external trappings of faith (v. 3).

Despite their religiosity, they are not concerned with justice for others (cf. 1:15–17; 59:2; Hos. 6:4–6; Amos 5:23, 24; Zech. 7:8–12). Instead of setting the day aside so that all can fast and pray, they want to rest while others work.

Expressions of their pride and hatred and a denial of the purpose of fasting, which is to humble oneself before God.

**heard on high.** God does not hear prayer when it is not sincerely offered in the spirit of love. Our sin can hinder the impact of our prayers (1 Pet. 3:7).

See 1:10–15; Amos 5:21–23; Mic. 6:7, 8.

**bow down ... sackcloth and ashes.** Conventional acts of mourning ceremonies that accompany fasting (Joel 1:13, 14). God looks for expressions of inner humility and brokenness before Him, rather than mere external devotion (Matt. 6:16). We find in 1 Sam. 15:22 the same idea: heart obedience to the Lord’s commands is better than rituals, even when those rituals are commanded by God.

This verse presents a different idea of fasting: to rescue the oppressed and provide for the needy (Matt. 25:34–40).

**to break every yoke.** Foreigners are not the only ones to place an oppressive yoke on God’s people, treating them like cattle; their own leaders are often oppressive as well.
Relatives, and secondarily people from the same tribe or area (1 Tim. 5:8). They should have compassion on the poor and the needy in their own community.

This word connects human responsibility and the coming of God’s kingdom. In the mystery of God’s providence, He creates the context in which He will act by stirring human acts of obedience.

**light ... glory.** The glorious kingdom of God (9:2; 60:1–3; Luke 1:78, 79) will dawn with God’s blessing and protection (2:5 note), and with His healing (30:26 note). It is the establishment of a new order (1:21 note) with the presence of the God of glory (4:2 note).

**rear guard.** Like the pillar of cloud and fire in the wilderness (4:5, 6; 52:12; Ex. 13:21; 14:20).

Then God will answer prayer (30:19; 65:24); Cf. note on v. 4.

**Here I am.** Typically this is a courteous answer given by a person who is ready to hear a message or follow instructions (e.g., Gen. 22:1, 7; Ex. 3:4; 1 Sam. 3:4). It is remarkable that God humbles Himself to respond in this way to the prayers of sinful people.

**yoke ... speaking wickedness.** These expressions represent oppression, contempt, and improper speech (Prov. 6:13).
See note on v. 8. The dawning of the new age brings ever greater brightness (2:5; 5:30 and notes).
They will be greatly blessed and productive (1:30, 31 note; cf. John 7:38). Rainfall was scarce in ancient Israel, so irrigation was necessary to grow a wide variety of plants.

The restored exiles will need the spiritual and economic resources to rebuild Judah (44:26, 28; 61:4; Ezek. 36:10; Amos 9:14, 15; Hag. 1:2–9; Acts 15:15–17). Even before the exile, however, Judah’s sin brings about ruins that need to be rebuilt (see 1:7).

**repairer of the breach.** The state of a city’s walls was crucial to its well-being and security, as well as its self-image (see 49:16; Neh. 1:3).

The Lord does not reject ritual as such. This day is the sign of the covenant (56:2 note).

**own ways ... own pleasure.** Their goals are social prestige, financial gain, and political importance (cf. 33:15 and note). The Sabbath is not just a day to refrain from following their own agenda; it is a day for pursuing the Lord’s agenda. Failure to observe the Sabbath is thus a key barometer of Israel’s spiritual health.

verse_quote: the heritage of Jacob your father.
note: The Abrahamic promises of land and blessing that were transmitted to Israel through Jacob (see Gen. 12:1–3).

LORD**’s hand is not shortened ... made a separation.** Unlike idols, which can do nothing to bless or curse, the Lord is still able to act. Yet He cannot simply be manipulated into action by the appropriate religious rituals (see 58:3). The people’s sins separate them from God such that He will not listen to their prayers or act to deliver them., 2
The people are defiled in their actions and in their words, bearing false witness against their neighbors (v. 4).
The comparison indicates wickedness that is not just an impulsive act but a lifestyle. They carefully cultivate evil plans that will harm their neighbors.
They do not hesitate to break God’s laws but run headlong toward evil (Prov. 1:16). Their actions result in discord and chaos, along with the shedding of innocent blood (Rom. 3:15–17).
As in the book of Proverbs, the “way” of a person denotes a settled pattern of behavior. Those who deny others peace will themselves be kept from it (48:22; 57:21).

–**13** The prophet includes himself among the sinful community, as in ch. 6. These transgressions are not simply the property of others; everyone in the community is implicated in them (v. 12). At least some are willing to confess the community’s sin and repent.
These words describe the experience of one cursed with blindness or darkness (Deut. 28:29; Job 5:14). The light promised in 58:10 has not yet dawned on this community.

verse_quote: growl like bears ... moan like doves.
note: Bears growl with anger, while the moaning of doves sounds like a sorrowful lament. Human emotions such as anger and lamentation, however, cannot achieve salvation, for they are unable to deal with the root problem, which is transgression.
The Lord’s refusal to act (59:1, 2) was fully justified; through their rebellion against Him, the people have forfeited any right to deliverance.

verse_quote: truth has stumbled in the public squares.
note: Their sin is not merely a private issue; the center of their society is infected with a profound spiritual malaise.

No one is able to help, except the Messiah (53:12; Rom. 5:7). No one can intercede, for the Lord has turned His face away from His people because of their sins. Until that fundamental breach in their relationship is dealt with, there can be no restoration. Yet no human can act as the mediator, since all are implicated through their own transgressions. God Himself will have to act alone to accomplish salvation, proving that His arm is not too short after all (see v. 1).

**righteousness.** His victorious salvation (46:13; 51:6, 8; 56:1).

Today, Christians put on this armor of God because God Himself in Christ has first worn it in our place (Eph. 6:13–17).

**put on ... wrapped.** The Lord of hosts will accomplish what no one else can do (42:13; 49:25; 52:10; Ex. 15:3).
The Lord will act both to judge and to save.

verse_quote: from the west ... from the rising of the sun.
note: His intervention is not limited to His own people but extends from the west to the east, as far as the distant coastlands (v. 18). However, the earlier chapters have promised that this intervention will not only result in the judgment of the nations but in their salvation as well (see 51:5).
He will come in the person of Jesus Christ, bringing salvation to all who repent and turn from their sins. Paul quotes this promise (Rom. 11:26, 27). See note on 35:9, 10.

The Lord’s covenant of grace is renewed through the gift of His promised Holy Spirit (42:6 note; Acts 2: 38, 39).

**Spirit.** The role of the Spirit of God is mentioned several times in the OT (32:15; 44:3; Jer. 31:31–34; Ezek. 37:14; Zech. 12:10). The Spirit works “by and with the Word in our hearts” (Westminster Confession 1.5). His continuing presence with His people was secured with the revelation of the NT (John 16:7, 13; 2 Cor. 5:5; Gal. 3:14; 4:6).

The imperative is addressed to Zion (v. 14).

**shine.** Zion receives and reflects God’s light (Luke 1:78, 79; Eph. 5:14; Rev. 21:23, 24).

verse_quote: darkness shall cover ... Lord will arise.
note:
Although the world is in darkness, God’s light shines on His people (John 1:15; Col. 1:13; 1 Pet. 2:9).

**his glory.** See 4:5; 40:5; John 1:14; Rev. 21:11.

See 2:2–4; 11:1; 42:16; 49:6. The prophecy has been fulfilled day by day since the coming of the gospel (Acts 9:15; 11:18).

**kings to the brightness.** They come to Christ (42:6; 49:6). The wise men who came to see Jesus were Gentiles (“nations”), if not “kings” in some sense.

See Hag. 2:7. The prophecy begins to be fulfilled with Darius’s contribution to the temple (Ezra 6:8, 9). It has a much greater fulfillment through the ascended Christ, the new temple (see John 2:19), who rules in the hearts of His people.

A desert tribe famous for caravans and trade (Gen. 37:28, 36; Judg. 6:5, 6).

**Ephah.** A tribe related to Midian (Gen. 25:4).

**Sheba.** This country is renowned for its wealth (1 Kin. 10:1, 2).

**gold and frankincense.** These were among the gifts that the wise men brought to the baby Jesus in Matt. 2:11.

For the sacrifices the restored temple will need a multitude of animals, which the nations will gladly provide.

**Kedar.** See note on 21:16.

**Nebaioth.** Related to the Ishmaelites (Gen. 25:13), and later known as Nabateans. Their capital was at Petra, fifty miles (80 km) south of the Dead Sea.

**My beautiful house.** The temple. See Ezra 7:27, where Ezra describes his mission in similar terms.

verse_quote: that fly like a cloud ... like doves to their windows.
note: Nothing can stand in the way of the motion of the clouds, and doves inevitably seek to return to their homes. Likewise, God’s people will inevitably and unstoppably return home, when the Lord calls them.

See 43:5–7, 14; 49:18; 51:5.

**ships of Tarshish.** See note on 23:5. The resumption of maritime trade is another way the glory of the new age is described in terms of Solomon’s splendor (1 Kin. 10:22).

**silver and gold.** See Hag. 2:7–9.

**he has made you beautiful.** Sharing the glory of the restored temple (v. 7). In the new covenant, the temple is a house made of living stones, formed of saints whom the Lord has clothed in His beautiful robes of righteousness (1 Pet. 2:5).

As Hiram, king of Tyre, helped build the first temple (1 Kin. 5), and Cyrus and Darius, kings of Persia, the second (Ezra 6), so also today people of many nations are building up the church, the temple of the Lord (Eph. 2:11–22).

**kings shall minister.** The postexilic community has been promised that foreign kings will depart (49:17); now it is asserted that foreign kings will serve Mount Zion and worship God. In His wrath against kings, God will remember mercy and save some of them.
Instead of attacking the city, the nations will bring tribute to the new Jerusalem (Rev. 21:25, 26).

Precious wood glorified Solomon’s temple as well (1 Kin. 6:15–18). This provides another connection between the former and latter glory (vv. 6, 9 and notes).

**place of my feet.** At first this expression referred to the ark of the covenant, which is the footstool of God’s invisible throne (Ps. 132:7; 1 Chr. 28:2); later, it referred to the temple, which housed the ark (Ezek. 43:7); and, finally, to the whole world, since the whole world is filled with God’s glory (66:1).

verse_quote: nurse at the breast of kings.
note: Figurative language for the wealth kings brought to Zion. In the past, the rulers of the world had oppressed Israel, but in the time to come they will support her.

Bronze and iron are important metals used for making tools and weapons in Isaiah’s day. Each material is replaced by one stronger or more valuable as a sign of the wealth of the nations flooding into Jerusalem. By analogy, the cultural and social life of the country will be raised beyond what Solomon knew. Whatever the interim fulfillments of this prophecy, it looks ultimately to the splendor of the New Jerusalem (Rev. 21:9–27; see also Ps. 48).

God’s salvation and Israel’s praise constitute the defense of the spiritual temple, Christ and His church (26:1 note; cf. Zech. 2:4, 5). The injustice and violence described in 59:3–8 will be gone forever.

God’s presence with His people (v. 1 note; Rev. 21:11, 23; 22:5). The sun and moon are perfectly adequate forms of light, but they pale into nothingness compared to the glory of God’s presence with His people. Just as there was light before the creation of sun and moon (Gen. 1:3–13), so there will be light after the sun and moon are no more (Rev. 21:23).

verse_quote: Your sun shall no more go down.
note: The problem with the sun and moon as sources of light is their changeableness. The sun goes down at night, while the moon waxes and wanes. In contrast, the Lord’s presence with His people in the eternal state is unchanging and unending.
Their salvation is God’s work from beginning to end (59:15–19).

The speaker is the messianic Servant. See 11:2; 42:1; 48:16; 59:21 and notes. The prophecy is fulfilled in the ministry of Christ, as He Himself declares (Luke 3:22; 4:18, 19). Isaiah is included (62:1) as a shadow or forerunner of Jesus.

**good news to the poor.** See Is. 40:9; 52:7; Ps. 9:18 note; Luke 7:22.

**proclaim liberty.** This phrase may be an allusion to the liberation of slaves in the Year of Jubilee (Lev. 25:10). It will resonated deeply with those in bondage in Babylon.

LORD**’s favor.** Through His death and resurrection, Jesus inaugurated the “day of salvation” (2 Cor. 6:2) in which the gospel is preached all over the world, and those who were estranged can find peace in Him (Eph. 2:12, 13; 3:5; 2 Tim. 1:10).

**day of vengeance.** Jesus stopped reading before this portion of Isaiah’s oracle, indicating that His work is split into two phases (Luke 4:18–20; cf. Mal. 4:6 with Luke 1:17). The time of healing belongs to His first coming; the time of judgment to the second (1 Thess. 1:10). See note on 34:8.

**to comfort all who mourn.** See Matt. 5:4. Those who mourn over the sins that surround them (59:9–15) will be comforted when the Lord redeems the remnant of His people.

verse_quote: a beautiful headdress instead of ashes.
note:
In Isaiah’s day, ashes are worn on the head as a sign of mourning. When the mourners are comforted, their ashes will be replaced by a headdress befitting their newfound joy.

**oaks of righteousness, the planting of the** LORD**.** Oaks are sturdy trees, not easily uprooted. The strength of the people will come from the fact that the Lord plants them, not from themselves (see 60:21).
Foreign servants will do the mundane farming chores, so that the Israelites can be free to become priests and ministers of God as He has always intended them to be (v. 6; cf. Ex. 19:5, 6).
See note on 60:5.

These words describe the experience of the Babylonian exile of the sixth century B.C. (30:3; 50:4–6).

**a double portion.** The firstborn inherits a double portion (Deut. 21:17). This image indicates that Israel will once again be the Lord’s firstborn (Ex. 4:22).
See notes on 24:5; 42:6; 55:3.

The blessings of the covenant are extended to the children (59:21).

**all who see ... blessed.** Alludes to the promise to Abraham (41:8; 51:2; Gen. 12:2, 3).

Zion is represented here as having received the blessings described in v. 3, e.g., joy and the garments of praise. To be “clothed” with something is a common metaphor for a change in status or condition (52:1; Zech. 3:3–5; Matt. 22:11; Rev. 19:7, 8).
The goal of God’s acts of salvation is to have a holy people for the praise of His glory (Eph. 1:4–6).

God acts not only for His own glory but for the good of His people (Rom. 8:28).

**burning torch.** This picture of salvation as a welcoming light is developed in 58:8; 60:1–3.

They witness the confirmation of the promises (2:2–4; 41:2 note; 52:10; 60:3; 61:11).

**a new name.** Like new clothes (61:10 note), the new name signifies a renewed relationship and enhanced privilege (vv. 4, 12; cf. 1:26; 56:5; 60:14, 18; cf. Gen. 17:5, 15; Rev. 2:17; 3:12).
The Lord shares His glory with His people. See 60:9.
The promised renaming process is underway, redefining Jerusalem’s status before God.

verse_quote: so shall your God rejoice over you.
note: The Lord does not redeem His people reluctantly and under obligation. He delights to do so because He rejoices in her (Zeph. 3:17).

An image for prophets (cf. 56:10 note, though there they are ineffective, false prophets).

**they shall never be silent.** Not because the danger is constant but because they are constantly declaring the Lord’s praise and interceding for the city (see 62:1).

verse_quote: has sworn by his right hand and by his mighty arm.
note:
That is, by Himself (see 14:24; 40:10 note; 41:10; 51:9; 52:10; 53:1).

**food for your enemies.** The curse (Lev. 26:16; Deut. 28:33) will be replaced by blessing.

verse_quote: drink it in the courts of my sanctuary.
note: Part of the annual tithe was brought to the temple in Jerusalem for a celebration, which might include alcoholic beverages (Deut. 14:22–26). In the restoration, the people will celebrate in God’s presence with no fear of their enemies.

verse_quote: Go through, go through ... build up, build up.
note:
These imperatives emphatically encourage the people to worship.

**gates.** These lead into the court of the sanctuary (v. 9).

**lift up a signal.** See 11:10; 49:22. Salvation is for the peoples as well as for Israel.
See note on 1:8.

See 4:3; Ex. 19:6; 1 Pet. 2:9, 10. Isaiah returns to the theme of a new name (see v. 2).

**Redeemed.** See note on 35:9.

The passage depicts God coming as the divine warrior (59:15–19), having accomplished the salvation of His people. This is the good news that the watchmen on the walls are to declare to their contemporaries (52:7–10).

**Edom.** Represents the ungodly and proud nations, as it does often in the OT (34:1–17, esp. v. 5; cf. Lam. 4:21, 22; Ezek. 35; Joel 3:19; Obad. 14, 15; Mal. 1:2–5).

**Bozrah.** An important city in Edom thirty miles (48 km) southeast of the Dead Sea.

God has won the victory without needing or receiving help from anyone else, and therefore does not need to share His glory with anyone (59:16).

**winepress ... stained.** An extended metaphor for the day of the Lord (Lam. 1:15; Joel 3:13; Rev. 14:17–20; 19:15). The winepress represents the battle, and the juice pressed out represents the casualties of war. The depiction also forms part of the blessing on Judah in Gen. 49:11, for in Jesus Christ God comes as a descendant of Judah to win the victory by shedding His own blood for the sake of His people. On the last day, Jesus Christ will return to win the final victory over all of His foes (Rev. 19:13–15).

verse_quote: day of vengeance ... my year of redemption.
note:
Alludes to the laws concerning slaves and property in the Jubilee year (Lev. 25). This idea of redemption is developed throughout Isaiah, especially in 61:1–63:6 (34:8; 35:9 and notes). The full redemption of God’s people necessarily includes the judgment of His enemies, though NT reveals that there is a chronological separation between the Messiah’s coming to bring salvation and His coming to bring judgment.

**had come.** The future is already seen through faith.
Isaiah will proclaim aloud (Pss. 51:13–15; 89:1; 145:7) the Lord’s mighty acts of the past, described as His “steadfast love” (_hesed_), His covenant loyalty to His people.

verse_quote: children who will not deal falsely.
note: What Israel was called to be, the faithful children of God (Ex. 4:22; Deut. 14:1), not what they actually became, the rebellious children described in 1:2–4.

Israel’s sufferings in Egypt (Ex. 2:23–25).

**angel of his presence.** See Ex. 14:19; 23:20–23. God Himself was with His people in angelic form, rescuing them from the enemies in miraculous ways. In v. 11, God’s presence in the midst of His people is by His Holy Spirit.

**carried.** Cf. Ex. 19:4; Deut. 1:31; 32:10–12.

Rebellion against God’s word brought the patience of God’s Spirit to an end, and the exile resulted (cf. 2 Chr. 36:15–21; Ps. 106:33; Acts 7:51; Eph. 4:30). Divine patience is longsuffering, but it will not restrain God’s judgment forever.

The period of the exodus and wilderness wanderings. This period, before Israel entered the land, is intensely relevant to those who are in exile in Babylon, and thus once again outside the land. In spite of the Lord’s faithfulness to them, they face the same temptations to doubt, grumble, and rebel against Him.

**shepherds of his flock.** Moses was this shepherd. Jesus is our shepherd (Heb. 3:1–6; 13:20).

verse_quote: Look down from heaven and see.
note: The prophet asks the Lord to renew His presence with His people as of old, restoring them from captivity. He appeals to the Lord’s compassion and mercy because the people have not merited the Lord’s aid.

God has always been the Father of His people (64:8; Ex. 4:22, 23; Jer. 3:4, 19); they are His children by adoption (Deut. 32:6; Rom. 8:15). They are rebellious children, and so might be disowned by earthly fathers such as Abraham or Israel (Jacob), but God will still be their father and their redeemer, buying them back from their self-inflicted bondage because of His grace and mercy.

**Abraham.** See 51:2.

God makes those who reject Him stray (Rom. 1:20–25; 2 Thess. 2:10–12), and may confirm them in their sin (6:10; Ex. 4:21; Ps. 95:8). Isaiah’s own preaching brings blindness and deafness to those who have rebelled against God (6:9, 10).
The Babylonians (Ps. 74:4–8).

verse_quote: like those over whom you have never ruled.
note:
The Lord’s reign over His people was manifest in His gift of the Promised Land. When they went into exile, the testimony to the relationship between the Lord and His people was erased.

**called by your name.** To signify ownership (Deut. 28:10; Jer. 14:9).

verse_quote: Oh that you would ... come down.
note: With eloquence Isaiah pleads with God not just to look down from heaven (63:15) but to come down, making His presence unmistakably clear, especially in the fires of judgment on His enemies (4:4, 5 and notes; Ex. 19:18; Heb. 12:18).

An allusion to God’s appearance on Mount Sinai after the exodus (Ex. 19:16–18; Deut. 10:21; Pss. 66:3–6; 106:22; see Ezek. 32:6–8 note). Such appearances often involve shaking the heavens and the earth, especially the mountains, which represent unshakable strength (Ps. 46:2).
Those who sincerely seek to serve the Lord, unlike the insincere followers in ch. 58.

Unfit to be in God’s presence (Lev. 13:45, 46; Hag. 2:13, 14).

**polluted garment.** Under the old covenant, garments stained by menstruation are defiled, as is anything else that comes into contact with a flow of life-fluids from the body (30:22 note; Lev. 15:19; Ezek. 36:17; cf. Phil. 4:7, 8). Since God is the Lord of life, nothing associated with a diminishment of life can enter His presence. Our problem is not merely our sinful acts but the fact that even our very best works are defiled before Him.

**We all fade like a leaf.** We are transitory mortals, while the Lord endures forever (40:7, 8). Like the wicked in Ps. 1, we are easily blown away in the wind.

See note on 63:16.

**clay ... work of your hand.** See notes on 22:11; 27:11; cf. Jer. 18:1–11; Rom. 9:20, 21. God is sovereign over the fate of all people; we exist to be shaped by Him.
Cf. the promises of 43:25; 54:7, 8.
The cities of Judah.

The object of Isaiah’s prayer in 63:15.

**our fathers.** The speakers are at least a generation removed from the fall of the temple in 586 B.C.

This is repeated for emphasis. God’s presence is salvation, and He is always ready to reveal Himself, even to those who are not looking for Him. See Is. 52:6.

**a nation that was not called by my name.** Gentiles (42:1; 49:6). Paul quotes this prophecy in Rom. 10:20. God’s salvation does not conform to human expectations; it originates in His free decision as the potter (64:8). Cf. Rom. 9:11, 12, 25, 26; 10:30, 31; 11:6, 17 on this important principle.

Unlike the people whose “hands are full of blood” (1:15), the Lord has reached out with love, entreating His own people to come to Him, but they will not come (John 1:11). Instead, they prefer to walk in ways that were not good (cf. Ezek. 20:25).

They did not hide their offensive, idolatrous acts (sinful patterns that they adopt­ed from surrounding nations), which are listed in the following verses.

**sacrificing in gardens.** Sacrifices associated with fertility religions (1:29 note).

They go there to consult the spirits of the dead (8:19; 29:4).

**pig’s flesh.** Eating pork was prohibited (66:3, 17; Lev. 11:7, 8; Deut. 14:8).

verse_quote: I am too holy for you.
note:
Their self-righteousness contrasts dramatically with the true state of affairs, described in 64:6.

**smoke ... fire.** They are a constant annoyance to God.
The principle of retribution applies in God’s judgment (Obad. 15; Gal. 6:7; 1 Pet. 1:17; Rev. 20:12, 13; 22:12).

verse_quote: your iniquities and your fathers’ iniquities.
note: Since they are sinning in exactly the same way as their ancestors, it is fitting that they should receive the same punishment.
The new wine in the cluster is the remnant for whose sake the whole is preserved (Matt. 13:29). The remnant is among both Israel (1:9 note) and the nations (56:6; cf. Gen. 18:22–33).
The kingdom will be theirs (14:1 note; 57:13; cf. Obad. 19–21).

A fertile plain on the Mediterranean coast south of Mount Carmel. It is a picture of how the Lord will transform creation (33:9; 35:1, 2 and notes).

**Valley of Achor.** South of Jericho (Josh. 7:24; Hos. 2:15).
Syrian gods whose names speak of the good fortune worshiping them is supposed to bring. Yet in reality, those who seek them are destined for destruction.

verse_quote: when I called, you did not answer.
note: The Lord will answer those who are not seeking Him (65:1), while those whom He has called but have not responded will go to destruction.

A contrast exists between the faithful remnant, who will be preserved, and the unfaithful idolaters, whose end is torment. Even though God’s people may face persecution and loss in the present, their final destiny is blessing.

To have your name remembered as a curse (“May you be like X”) is an even worse fate than being forgotten.

**another name.** See note on 62:2. A name of blessing rather than curse.
The Hb. word translated “truth” is “amen”; see 2 Cor. 1:20; Rev. 3:14; also John 14:6; 1 John 5:20. That is, the God who is true.

verse_quote: new heavens and a new earth.
note:
This prophecy awaits the second coming of Christ (2 Pet. 3:13; Rev. 21:1). In the meantime, through faith the saints experience in part the blessing of the age to come (42:9; 43:19 and notes).

**the former things.** The adversities and disgrace brought on by sin, especially the judgment of the exile (41:22 note).
It will be altogether new with no remembrance of the sins of the old city (Rev. 21:1, 2), thereby accomplishing God’s purpose for it in the beginning (see Ps. 48:1).

Here the blessings of the new heavens and earth are described in pictorial terms as the experience of the blessings promised for obedience to the Sinai covenant, such as long life, freedom from invasion, and safety from wild animals (cf. Deut. 28:30).

**65:20 infant ... old man.** Premature death of infants or persons in midcareer can provoke the thought that life is meaningless. Such early death, as also the transfer of one person’s reward to another person who has not earned it (v. 22), is part of God’s judgment on sin. God promises to remove this curse from His people (Amos 5:11 note). This is possible because Christ has come and fulfilled the terms of the Law, meriting its blessings for Himself and all those who are in Him.

verse_quote: like the days of a tree.
note: In Ps. 1, the righteous are compared to a well-watered tree, while the wicked are driven away by the wind like chaff (see 64:6).

See 11:6, 7. The images are not simply about the future of animals but the future of humanity, indicating that people will no longer oppress one another as they have in the past (see 59:14, 15).

**dust shall be the serpent’s food.** Alludes to Gen. 3:14. The curse on Satan is carried out, with the resulting blessings for redeemed humanity.

Cf. 30:16; 37:16. Elsewhere the ark of the covenant is called God’s footstool, but the entire earth is small enough to fulfill that role. Any temple constructed by human hands cannot possibly contain the Lord.

**the place of my rest.** Cf. Num. 10:35, 36. The ark represents the presence of God with His people.

verse_quote: he who is humble and contrite in spirit.
note: Even though the heaven of heavens cannot contain His majesty, the Lord stoops low to enter a relationship with the humble and the repentant (see 57:15).

The Lord hates empty religious expressions as much as outright paganism—even when people are (externally) following the laws that He has given them explicitly (Jer. 7:21–23 note). Heartfelt obedience is always better than sacrifice (see 58:5; 1 Sam. 15:22). Mere external conformity to God’s demands without the desire to love and serve Him from the heart is ultimately equivalent to paganism.

**66:3 kills a man.** Possibly an allusion to child sacrifice (cf. Jer. 7:31; Ezek. 23:39).

**breaks a dog’s neck.** Only certain animals are prescribed for sacrifice. The dog is not even permitted for food (56:10 note; Lev. 11:26).

**pig’s blood.** See 65:4.

**66:4 bring their fears upon them.** Pagan idolatry offers the promise of security and blessing in exchange for the rote external performance of religious ceremonies. People often see biblical religion in much the same way, believing that going through the motions is enough to please the Lord. However, such religious rituals are not simply valueless—they are counterproductive, bringing upon the worshipers the very things that they fear most.

**when I called, no one answered.** See 65:12. The essence of true religion is a responsive heart to God’s Word.

The opposition reflected in ch. 65 between God’s servants and nominal Israel has intensified to the point where the faithful are being cast out of the community for the sake of the Lord. The same thing happens in the NT (see Luke 6:22, 23).

**Let ... joy.** Such an expression of praise by rebellious people is hypocritical righteousness.

**shall be put to shame.** Humiliation is the fate of the persecutors. See v. 10 for the fate of the persecuted.
The Lord is coming from His earthly palace to render judgment upon His enemies within His own community.

The birth of the new community will be sudden and miraculous, and no human effort will contribute to it. Christ laid the foundation of the church in His lifetime, especially in the week of His death and resurrection (John 2:19).
God’s purposes will not be frustrated or begun and left unfinished.

This points to the unexpected logic of Jesus’ beatitudes (see Matt. 5:4). Those who mourn over Jerusalem’s state of disgrace and internal turmoil (see v. 5) are called to rejoice all the more at the prospect of the new heavens and new earth where such things will be gone forever.
See note on 60:16.

Mother Jerusalem (vv. 8, 10).

**like a river.** The image of a river of blessing flowing out from the presence of God is ubiquitous in the Scriptures (Gen. 2:10–14; Ps. 46:4; Ezek. 47:1–12; Rev. 22:1, 2). In an arid climate, it is a potent picture of abundance and peace.

**glory of the nations.** See 60:5–7.

verse_quote: As one whom his mother comforts.
note: The Lord likens His tender love to that of a mother comforting her child. The same image of comfort began this section in 40:1.

verse_quote: your bones shall flourish like the grass.
note: Reversing the image of 40:7, where the focus is on the transitory nature of grass, here the focus is on the rapidity with which grass springs up.

These depict lightning and storm clouds respectively (Deut. 33:26; Ps. 18:10; Jer. 4:13), common accompaniments of God’s appearance (10:17, 18; 29:6; Ezek. 1:4; 32:6–8 note). Isaiah earlier prayed for God to come in this way to bring judgment to His enemies and vindication for His people (64:1–3).
The Lord appears as a warrior (27:1; 34:5; Rev. 19:11–18). See notes on 9:6; 13:4; 40:10; 42:13.
See v. 3; 65:2–5. These are pagan practices.

The works and thoughts of those to be gathered. The Lord’s judgment is never based on guesswork or circumstantial evidence; He knows the hearts of people (see 1 Sam. 2:3).

**all nations and tongues.** There will be universal acknowledgement of the Lord’s kingdom (Zech. 8:23; Rev. 7:9, 10).

**glory.** God’s glory in His temple (Ezek. 11:22, 23; 44:4).

See 7:14; 11:10, 12; 55:12, 13. The Lord’s great works have not been done in secret.

**survivors.** The true worshipers who survive persecution (v. 5; Matt. 24:9–14) bring God’s glory to the nations (v. 18).

**Tarshish.** See note on 23:5. Probably Spain.

**Pul, and Lud.** In North Africa.

**Tubal.** South of the Black Sea in modern Turkey (Ezek. 38:2, 3; 39:1).

**Javan.** The people of Asia Minor or Greece (Ezek. 27:13, 19; Joel 3:6).

**declare ... nations.** The Gentiles will submit themselves to the Lord and rejoice in His mighty acts (24:16 note). This promise finds fulfillment in the book of Acts as the gospel goes out from Jerusalem to Judea, Samaria, and the ends of the earth (Acts 1:8).
The Gentiles will bring dispersed Israel back to the temple (2:2–4; 43:5; 60:4, 9; Rom. 11:11–14).

See note on 65:17 (cf. 2 Pet. 3:13; Rev. 21:1).

**your offspring and your name.** God’s people will never again suffer reproach, but they will enjoy everlasting glory (43:1 note; 65:18, 19; cf. Jer. 31:35, 36).
There will be universal worship of God at His appointed times (cf. Zech. 14:16).

Jerusalem’s garbage dump becomes symbolic of perpetual punishment and anguish (30:33 note; Mark 9:47, 48). As Jesus taught, there will be a final separation of the righteous and the wicked, the one going to everlasting joy and the other going to everlasting torment (Matt. 13:24–30, 47–50).
